title: Why Dirk Willems Turned Back
description: The Man on Thin Ice. Christianity’s Crisis Was 1500 Years in the Making
text: Episode 01      |    Dirk Willems Why Dirk Willems Turned Back The Man on Thin Ice. Christianity’s Crisis Was 1500 Years in the Making 49 min 1450 – 1569 Vienna, Austria; Asperen, Netherlands; Hermannsdenkmall, Germany About This Episode Why would a man turn back to save the very person pursuing him, knowing it could cost him his life? Welcome to the first episode of Anabaptist Origins. In this documentary series, our hosts Dean Taylor, Stephen Russell, and Reagan Schrock tell the story of an incredible movement in the 16th century that stood against the relentless tide of the state church. But this didn’t happen in a vacuum. Important individuals and events shaped the environment for centuries before the state of affairs forced the early Anabaptists to take their costly stand. How did the humble early church turn into a powerful machine fused with the state, and what did people like Constantine and Charlemagne have to do with it? Who were the Bogomils and the Waldensians? How did the printing press, Erasmus, and John Wycliffe influence society? Who was Jan Hus? What did he do to deserve such an extreme punishment by fire? Join our hosts as they lay the historical foundation that helps us understand why a few young people in the 16th century thought it was necessary to leave their comfortable lives behind and be outcasts for Christ. Anabaptist Origins is a 10-part documentary series produced by Anabaptist Perspectives that seeks to tell the history of the Anabaptist movement in a way that brings it to life. View Episode Credits Here: anabaptistorigins.org/credits/ Read the Transcript 0:00 | Cold Open: The Question History remembers this place for a question. He was running, a hunted man: imprisoned, tortured, and condemned. Not for a crime of violence, but simply for what he believed. He was an Anabaptist, and his name was Dirk Willems. Somehow, Dirk escaped from prison. The castle moat, just here, was frozen, and he fled across the thin ice. Freedom was within his grasp. And then his pursuer fell through, and Dirk Willems turned back. He re-crossed the treacherous ice and saved the very man who would lead him to the fire of his execution. Why did Dirk Willems turn back? That question, “Why did Dirk Willems turn back?” is one that takes us 500 years into the past. I’m Reagan Schrock. With historical theologian Dean Taylor and church history teacher Stephen Russell, we traveled across Europe to the actual sites where the Anabaptist story unfolded, from Zurich, Switzerland, to the lowlands of the Netherlands. Across ten episodes, we trace the first hundred years of a movement that refused the sword, even when it cost them everything, and followed Jesus even when following Jesus was fatal. This is Anabaptist Origins. 1:22 | At the Moat, Asperen So this single act of mercy that Dirk Willems did, just right over there in that moat, has outlasted empires. But the big question is: why did Dirk Willems turn back? One possible way of answering that is that he was an Anabaptist. But what does that mean? What does it mean to be an Anabaptist? That’s what our series is going to be looking at as we go on. To even answer the question, we need to go back further in time. We need to go back to the time of Christ, to the time of the Roman Empire, and to look at what was going on in Europe when the Anabaptists came on the scene. And to do that, we should go to some of the locations that give us the context that led to this event here. To understand why Dirk Willems turned back, we need to go back. Back 2,000 years, way before any cathedral. Dirk Willems was an Anabaptist, and historians usually date the beginning of Anabaptism to 1525. But the Anabaptists would not have wanted to consider themselves as starting the church in 1525. Rather, they saw themselves as part of the faith that was handed to them from the Apostles. They were people of Jesus Christ who were trying to put the plan of Jesus, his plan for humanity, into practice. 3:00 | The Hermannsdenkmal: Empire and the Kingdom of God There was another empire that was started at that time, around Augustus Caesar, and we came to this amazing spot to talk about that very thing. We are here at the Hermannsdenkmal. In 9 A.D., this is the place where the Roman army had their greatest defeat. It was here that the general Arminius, a general trained by the Roman army, turned their tactics into an ambush that lasted three days and ended up costing three Roman legions. It was a terrible defeat for Rome. In the ancient histories of Augustus, it was recorded that in mourning he would grow his beard out and just kept saying, “Varus, give me my legions.” Well, that other kingdom, the kingdom that was started in a manger and led to the Apostles, grew. But it grew by martyrdom. It grew by humility, across different cultures and different languages and different ways. The message of Jesus and its simple ways took over an empire, until finally it grew and grew to a place where the empire said, “We’re going to use this for our means.” And that’s the change that happened. St. Augustine gives us this in his book, The City of God: this idea of the city of God and the city of man. Even in his book he’s wrangling with how to combine these together, and different ones have written about this. In The City of God he says: “Accordingly, the two cities have been formed by two loves, the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God, the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.” Yes, those tensions between the city of God and the city of man are ancient, and Augustine never fully resolved it either. And so through time, the cross and its kingdom went in a way of sacrifice and peace. The empire has also tried to use military strength and, when it could, any religion it could to force its power over people. 5:15 | Charlemagne and the Imperial Gospel As a matter of fact, this place was built for a different reason, not just the defeat of Rome. Right here in this very area also was a man by the name of Charlemagne. Charlemagne, Charles the Great, conquered the German pagans, but his way was very brutal, and he did it under the name of Christianity. In the 700s, Charlemagne led the Saxon wars, forcing the pagans to convert to Christianity. He forced them into baptisms, and if they would not convert to his form of Christianity, the sentence was death. This kind of thing continued for centuries. Not far from here, in the town of Verden, Charlemagne massacred 4,500 people for not accepting his imperial gospel. Now, I wish I could say that people don’t behave this way anymore, that these are just remnants of the past, of ignorant people who didn’t know better. But here’s the problem: without repentance, without a genuine change, the same theology, given similar circumstances, often creates similar results. A little over a thousand years from the time Charlemagne was massacring people here, the Germanic people put up this statue with the sword raised to heaven, over the site of the defeat of the Romans, as a sign of the rising of the Germanic people. And that idea, Hermann the German, which is what this represents, represented a mix of church and state and military power in a way that affected the nations again. These empires came and they fell, but the church is still praying the same. The church is still living the faith that was handed to them from the Apostles. And still to this day, the plan for humanity given to us from Jesus Christ is meant to change the world in a positive way. 7:14 | The Holy Roman Empire On Christmas Day in the year 800, the Pope crowned Charlemagne as Emperor of the Romans. This Holy Roman Empire, as it was later called, endured for over a thousand years. Its emperors had an ever-shifting relationship with the church, and it was within this tangled imperial world that the Reformation and the Anabaptist movement arose. In the Reformation era, the emperors of this sprawling realm mostly came from the Habsburg dynasty. They ruled from the city of Vienna, now in modern-day Austria. 7:48 | Vienna: Church and State Fused Well, here we are in Vienna, the heart of the Habsburg Empire, and this is a really good image for some of the things that happened. In the early days, the church was very focused on following Jesus, doing what he had told them to do. In fact, during that time they were persecuted by the Roman Empire. And then around the 300s, Constantine became Emperor, and gradually there started to be a change, where the church and the state started coming closer and closer together. Eventually this brought a lot of corruption. In fact, the church reached the pinnacle of its power around 1200, when almost every prince and king in Europe owed allegiance to the Pope. So it went from a persecuted people to a people eventually considered part and parcel of the empire and its goals. So let’s go further back. How was this originally? How did this all start for the church, especially the early church, in contrast to what we’re seeing here? Well, I would like to go the whole way back. God, who is love, freely created the world so he could share his love with creatures. Unfortunately, we fell. But God, who is love, sent his Son, who lived, died, and rose again to give us new life. It’s out of that that the church starts, in roughly AD 30. At Pentecost the Spirit comes and fills the people who are the church. And from that point on there’s a dynamic expansion of the church, not just in the Roman Empire but beyond. At the very first, the Romans opposed the church. They felt it was undermining their empire. But when we finally get to Constantine, that changes. Following that whole Constantine era, the radicals still existed. The true believers and followers of Jesus still existed in history. It’s just very difficult to find them, because usually all we have are the writings of their persecutors. Through the ages there have been these people, within the Catholic church and outside it, not necessarily in this group or that group, but people wanting to follow the teachings of Jesus and trying to walk it out. Let’s go get a cup of coffee and mention a few of the significant ones. I want to give a little backdrop of where we’re sitting before we continue this conversation. If we look that way, that’s the gateway into the palace complex for what would have been the Habsburg Empire. This old city square goes back to Roman times. But right across from it is a church called St. Michael’s Church. You about can’t get a clearer picture of church and state fused together, because this was the seat of the government. This square is the Habsburg Empire. This is where you enter the palace complex, and right there is this church going back to the 1200s. It really symbolizes exactly what we’ve been talking about, and how we got to this point. That’s the fusion of church and state we’re thinking about in this episode. So pick up the story from there. What happens next? 11:18 | Believers Through the Ages: Bogomils and Waldensians The mistake we could make as historians is to think the church disappears, and then suddenly Martin Luther brings it all back in the 1500s. The fact is, through all time since Pentecost, Jesus has promised us the church would never fail. And so there have been these believers and gatherings always, in all different places. It’s difficult sometimes to find the records. Many times what we have is just what their enemies said of them, and they usually tried to make it sound as bad as possible. But some of those accounts are significant, and they do show a theological problem: that combination of church and state, and with it a power and a coercion that was just very ugly. This happened all across the Christian world. It happened in the Roman Catholic sections, and it happened in the Byzantine Orthodox places as well. When we look at the historic account of how the church responded to people who thought differently, it’s kind of sad. For example, in the Balkans there was a movement called the Bogomils, and they taught a simple faith centered on Christ’s teaching. We do know that. They were branded heretics, but unfortunately most of what we know of them comes, again, from their persecutors. We do know they rejected infant baptism, icons, and military service, and for this they were condemned by the Orthodox Church. As a matter of fact, in the 1100s two Cappadocian bishops had enough of this state church system and left. They were branded as heretics, and a regional synod at Constantinople in 1143 ruled that they should be executed, burned at the stake. These kinds of things continued. Here in the West there were the gatherings of the Waldensians. Now, one thing with the Waldensians: it’s not always just one people. When you’re looking into this time period, “Waldensian” has become kind of a label. There’s the classic story of Peter Waldo wanting to preach. In the early records, he’s not wanting to rock the boat much at all. It’s simply: I just want to preach. I want to go and preach the gospel. I want to be poor. I want to walk around and tell people about Jesus. That later developed, and as groups came out from him, and others gathered like that, they were branded Waldensians. And the Roman Catholic churches of the West suppressed this movement, and ones related to it, surprisingly strongly. Peter Waldo did request the possibility of preaching. His own bishop said no. He appealed to the Pope, and the Pope said yes, if your local bishop approves it. And Waldo and his friends were not willing to do that. So they went against church authority. 14:17 | Francis of Assisi Then you come maybe thirty or forty years later, and we get to Francis of Assisi. He wanted to serve God as well. He went to the Pope and asked for permission. He was denied twice and eventually allowed. So he was willing to obey, but persistent. He started a new order which operated within the church. This was desperately needed, because there wasn’t an established seminary system. Some men who wanted to be priests went to the university, and they were usually well trained. But a lot of them were trained by their own village priest, and there was a decline in the ability to preach. Around 1200 there was a big need for preaching, and Francis met that need. Whenever anybody heard about a Franciscan in a nearby village, they’d go down and say, you need to come to us next. They wanted to hear God’s Word preached. They knew the story, but they wanted to hear the Scriptures laid out for them. So Francis was extremely important in helping the Christians of Europe understand their faith better. When the Black Death came in the middle 1300s, many of the other priests fled the cities out of fear. The Franciscans tended to stay and take care of their people, and they suffered an immense number of deaths. 15:56 | John Wycliffe So let’s take it to England, to John Wycliffe. We’re starting to see the Word of God come out, people saying: we’ve got to somehow get these Scriptures into our hands. Tell us a little bit about John Wycliffe. Wycliffe is very interesting. He was a professor at Oxford, so he was reading the Bible not in Greek and not in Hebrew. He was reading the Vulgate, the Latin Bible. And he came to see at least four areas where the church was wrong. One was that he emphasized there are two kingdoms. Now, he didn’t think about it the way we do. He said there are two kingdoms: one is the secular, the other is the ecclesiastical, and they should never overlap. They overlapped completely in the Middle Ages. So that was one critique: they should not be overlapped, and when they do, they lose their authority. So the Catholic church actually ruling little city-states was wrong. That was his first point. Then he said there are the elect, and only the elect go to heaven. But we don’t know who they are. We have some clues, though, and one clue, once again this is the Middle Ages, is poverty. And who are the poor people in the Middle Ages? The peasants. So Wycliffe wasn’t saying no nobleman was elect, but it’s a guess that mostly the elect are the peasants. And who is not elect? The wealthy church. Ouch. They probably didn’t like that. The rulers and the church people could read Latin. But if the peasants are the elect, they need the Bible in their language. The Bible is for God’s people. God’s people are the elect, and probably most of them are the peasants. So: separation of the two kingdoms, and the elect need to have the Bible in their language. So he translated the Bible into English. All those things went over reasonably well. And then finally he said, “I do not believe in transubstantiation.” That’s the Catholic teaching that the bread and the wine become the body and blood of Christ, and that this is how you receive Christ. That was a step too far. Just think about it: if this is how I believe I receive Christ, and he says nothing is happening there… He lost his backing among the nobles. He was sent away from Oxford, went to a little parish church, and died there. 18:42 | The Lollards and Jan Hus Talk about church and state together. This Habsburg palace is amazing; you can’t get a more striking visual on this than here. This is the old city center, going back to Roman times. When they were re-laying the tiles, they kept finding old Roman road underneath. This would be the gateway into the palace complex, the old government building, and right here is St. Michael’s, which this plaza is actually named after. You can see Michael striking down what appears to be Satan. Back at the cafe you were telling us about John Wycliffe, saying God’s Word is for all people. What happens next? Wycliffe had disciples, and this whole preaching to the poor continued. People from the modern-day Czech Republic, the Bohemian areas, came and studied at Oxford, and they would have encountered these teachings. His followers were called the Lollards, which was a derogatory word, just like “Anabaptist” was. It was a name given by their enemies, and most people think it means something like murmuring or stammering. Nonsense. That’s kind of mean. So they took this message back, and it started to gain ground in the Bohemian area. One of the people who caught on to this was Jan Hus. He began to read the Scriptures and to preach, and he was an amazingly popular preacher. People would flock into his church to hear him, and he was preaching upon the Word of God. He talked about a reform that needed to come. He also taught that the sacrament should be given in both kinds, as the Bible says, and at the time this was a very important issue. The argument then was that if it’s the real presence, and it’s all within the wafer, why would you need the wine when you can just take the wafer? What era is this? When is he preaching? He was burned at the stake in 1415. So a few hundred years after this church was built, for perspective. So he’s standing up to institutions that are extremely old and established. When I study that Czech area, you find people who follow as very radical followers of Jesus. You hear pockets of non-resistance in the different movements that follow after him, and it brings in things that challenge this concept of Christendom: can’t we get back to the simple teachings of Jesus? Can’t we have what the Bible teaches, even in the sacraments? He’s making these kinds of challenges, and those things begin to catch on. 21:46 | The Printing Press So we’re walking through an area that really illustrates the power of empire at the time. And yet we look at this, the Habsburg Empire, which doesn’t exist anymore. What happened? There were ideas starting to spread that very much outlasted this empire and the church-state arrangement they had here. What was one of the key pieces of technology at the time that really made a difference in the flow and spread of ideas? Well, up until the middle 1400s, everything that was written had to be done by hand. Manuscripts were copied, and that meant new ideas went out very slowly. Books were expensive, and the people who bought them were mostly either wealthy or university-educated. But in the middle of the 1400s the printing press was developed. It took a bit of time, but because of it, all of a sudden you could print large numbers of books and sell them for a small price. At least relatively speaking. Reasonable, compared to doing it all by hand. So the ideas of Wycliffe went down to Bohemia, and Hus was not quite as radical as Wycliffe, but he thought these ideas should be discussed. They couldn’t be at that time, not widely. Hus’s effect was on Bohemia alone, because they spoke the same language, so the ideas could spread within that small area. But once the printing press comes, people can start to buy books, not just the Bible, and hear what kinds of things are being discussed. They printed books, but they also printed little pamphlets, and I think it’s interesting: in a way, that was the internet of their day. For instance, if we were in a little village, there was a man, in English called a chapman, who sold books and pamphlets and traveled around. One day the chapman would come in and sell the latest writing of Luther. The storekeeper would buy it, all the villagers would come together, he’d read it to them, and they’d start discussing it. Maybe two weeks later the chapman would come back the other way, a Catholic had responded, and now he had the Catholic response. You’re describing almost an old-style internet forum discussion. Kind of. And this is really important, because when they’re writing some of these new ideas, pre-Reformation and as the Reformation starts, you’re going up against an established order that feels very permanent. How could you ever question this awesome display of power? And yet it’s gone now. The Holy Roman Empire is gone. I like that you brought up the tracts, because when you read of the early Reformation, Martin Luther’s famous act of putting his theses on the Wittenberg door: the next day it was taken and put into these little tract forms, and it went viral. If it weren’t for this small, easy-to-press format, the Reformation probably wouldn’t have caught on so quickly. It would have stayed a lot more local. And it wasn’t just the pamphlets. Not everybody could read, but the priests would get these, and they would be drawn one way or the other, and so you would start to hear this preached over the pulpit even if you couldn’t read. The Word of God comes with a promise. It’s a living book, and when people were allowed to have the Scriptures, or discussions about the Scriptures, it woke up a world that said: another way is possible. We could live these teachings of Jesus. We could live like this. Why are we not? I agree. I think that was one of the primary things that led up to the Reformation and caused the world to see things differently. 26:10 | Erasmus and the Greek New Testament One of the things I love about being in these old European cities is you come across things like this, a visual anchor for what you were just telling us about. With this spread of new ideas and the printing press, who were some of the early thinkers and writers really taking advantage of it, and what effect did they have on church life and this whole church-and-state question? Well, originally the vast majority of what was printed was probably the Bible or some kind of devotional book, which makes me think of The Imitation of Christ. That would have been written right around the same time, and it became a very popular book to print. Even today it’s probably the most popular devotional book in the world. But the man who really takes the press and uses it, at first anyway, is Erasmus. He gathers all the Greek manuscripts he can find and produces a critical edition of the Greek New Testament. He also writes paraphrases and commentary, and this goes out. It can go out to just about anybody, because it’s printed on the printing press, so it’s cheaper, and many copies are made at one time. A Bible would take a whole year for one man to copy by hand. Think about that. So Erasmus puts together the first critical edition of the New Testament that was actually published. The Catholics had printed one earlier, but they were checking it so thoroughly that Erasmus got his out first. He got hold of theirs when it came out and used it to correct his original, because they had more manuscripts than he did. So this is really important. Erasmus was a committed Catholic, I think, but he cared about the corruption of the church, and so he makes fun of the Pope, Julius II, who was known for sitting on his war horse in armor more than standing in front of an altar. He took the name Julius from Julius Caesar. What era are we talking? When did Erasmus live? He and the early reformers are contemporaries. So they buy his New Testament, they read it, and they find little things, or big things. One of them, the one I always bring up: at the beginning of both Matthew and Mark, Jesus says, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” And in the Latin Bible it said, “Do penance,” because the kingdom of God is at hand. Oh my, that’s a big difference. There were other things, but that was maybe the most important one. So Erasmus provides the springboard for people who are concerned and think the church has been corrupted. Some of them get a bit of humor from his writings. He has Julius II, who was still alive at the time, die in one of his books and come up to the pearly gates, and with his spear pound on the gates of heaven. Saint Peter looks down and says, “Who are you?” And he says, “I’m Pope Julius.” And Peter says, “You don’t look like a pope.” You can imagine how that would have gone viral. Wait a minute. How did he get away with this? He’s a Catholic, and here’s an institution that’s been around for a very long time. If someone comes along and starts writing things like this while still being part of it, what were the ramifications? Was he actually able to do this? Many people weren’t putting their names or dates or publishers on these things. The book I’m talking about is called In Praise of Folly, which you can still get and read today. I don’t think he put his name on it, but from the style, everyone knew it was him. You just couldn’t really pin it on him. He was bold then. Oh yes. Really taking advantage of what was the mass media of the day. And then, when Luther and Zwingli get hold of his Greek New Testament and start translating, the more conservative Catholics throw an accusation at Erasmus: you haven’t left the Catholic Church, but you laid the egg that Luther hatched. And this is very true. It gave Luther a definite, clear indication of what the original said. This is our foundational document for the church. Erasmus wasn’t the only one who knew things had to change. Many were amused at what he had done to the Pope. This is the Renaissance, so “back to the sources” was the cry. And setting it up: in 1453 the Ottomans took over Constantinople, where there were many ancient manuscripts, not just the biblical writers but also the classics. When the city fell, those documents started to come into circulation, and it caused an excitement. So now you have Erasmus showing people the source of the main source of all things, the Bible. People said: you mean we can actually dig in deeper? With Zwingli and Luther we have their own accounts of getting hold of the ancient texts like this. I’m starting to see how significant this is, because as we’ll see in following episodes, the first Anabaptists are constantly saying: go back to Scripture. What does the Scripture say? I know the city council wants us to do this, but show me in the Bible. That would have been very hard to do a hundred years before, or even less, without these translations. It gave these new thinkers material to actually process: what does the Bible say? And it gave the common people access too, because they started translating the Bible into the language of the common people. We often don’t realize this, but it forced the Catholics to do the same. Soon after the first English Protestant Bible came out, the Catholics who had been expelled from England, because England was becoming Protestant, were living in what we call Belgium today, and they started translating the first English Catholic Bible. Basically, they saw which way the wind was blowing. People were asking for this. There was all this new material coming to the surface, and the church had to deal with it. What do we do with this Erasmus fellow? Which, again, I’m amazed he could question institutions this large and actually get away with it. 33:53 | The Anabaptists and the Bible Not a lot of Catholics, and not a lot of Protestants, could read, or at least there were a large number who couldn’t. But one of the things the Anabaptists did was teach their people how to read, because they really wanted each one to have a Bible, or at least a New Testament, that he could read. Then you could get together and discuss it. It was expected very early on among the Anabaptists that everyone got a Bible if he could afford it, and they taught them how to read. Before many of them knew how to read, the Anabaptist leaders would teach them important Scriptures, like the Great Commission, by memorization, so that when they were questioned by either the Catholics or the Protestants, they could quote Scripture. Sometimes the people asking them, “Why are you an Anabaptist?” were amazed that even though these people couldn’t read, they could quote Scripture. That’s how important it was to the Anabaptists. And what’s fascinating: once the common people started to read these Scriptures, it opened a whole different world of questions. Up until the Middle Ages and beyond, very detailed, speculative theology was common everywhere. Now people were able to ask some very simple questions. Jesus talks about living a life of poverty, about giving to the poor, about loving your enemies. What about this simple stuff? And with Erasmus himself, people often call him a humanist, and it’s not in the sense of a secular humanist, but in the sense of caring about the human person, the things of justice and daily life that people cared about. He was able to speak to that, and it resonated with them. 36:03 | Faith and the Sacraments The other thing that was very significant with Erasmus and the early ones concerned the sacraments, which is what many of the debates were over. One of the things that rose to the surface was faith. The concern in church history had been to get away from the idea that a minister had to be perfect for the sacraments to work. They didn’t want people saying, if the minister has sin in his life, the sacrament didn’t work, and they would cite the ancient councils, the Donatist controversies with Augustine, that sort of thing. So there was this teaching that it goes beyond the person having to be perfect, but it developed into the Latin phrase ex opere operato: “by the act it happens.” No matter what. It literally became mechanical. That was much of the defense of infant baptism and of the way ordinations were done. Even when, throughout the Middle Ages in both East and West, there were clearly documented payoffs to become bishop or archbishop: well, ex opere operato. We went through all the proper steps, so God had to act in that sacrament because of his word and his promises. People began to challenge this and said: without faith, how can we have just an empty, mechanical thing? This was one of the challenges Erasmus and others raised. It wasn’t just Luther. It wasn’t just the Protestants. There were many within the Catholic Church rising up and asking: how can we do this mechanically? 37:42 | Return to Asperen: The Rest of Dirk’s Story So we’ve been seeing the conditions in Europe, that fusion of church and state. We started this episode with the story of Dirk Willems, and we want to end it in that same place and tell the rest of his story. I want to point out that this is a recent excavation. They found the castle where he was held as a prisoner, the one he escaped from. It’s overgrown right now, but this is the old castle wall running along here, and it’s still being excavated. That’s only happened in the last few years. Dirk Willems lived in Asperen, and he had been baptized as a young man into the Anabaptist faith. It was known that he was an Anabaptist. But King Philip of Spain had recently become not just the King of Spain but also the ruler of the Netherlands. His father had passed an edict which said you cannot change your religion; that is not permissible. And Philip really enforced that rule. Dirk Willems was a known Anabaptist, and now the authorities were ordered to allow no one to be of any religion other than Catholicism. The authorities took him and put him in prison here at the castle. We’re probably walking where it originally stood. Maybe the courtyard, perhaps. Yes, and there was a moat all the way around it. Some of this water back here is still part of that original moat. It’s now just a pond, but the historian confirmed it is part of the original moat. In the old etching you can see both the moat around the castle itself and the larger moat around the entire city wall. After he was taken prisoner, he was probably given some help by a sympathetic worker in the castle to get away. Our local historian told us we know for sure he headed out in this direction. That means this part of the moat, which is still here, is where he crossed the lightly frozen ice, got to the other side, and could have escaped to the next town if he wanted to. But then he realized that the man following him had fallen through. He stopped, and he came back, and he saved that man’s life. Both of them got to the other shore. The bailiff, who was the thief-catcher’s superior, was standing on the far side, and he told him: you have to hold him. He has broken the law, and you have to hold him. And so the thief-catcher did. Just 200 yards back that way are the castle ruins where Dirk Willems was recaptured, and they brought him here, to this church. As far as we know, there was a prison up in the top. This is where Willems was held after he was recaptured. Most likely, as far as we can tell, he was brought to this very spot. I asked earlier whether this is the original door from that time. It’s from around 1700, so a little after Dirk. The same is true of the stocks. But it’s a very accurate representation of what he may have experienced while he sat here, waiting through the proceedings between his capture and his eventual death. 41:18 | The Execution What happens next is tragic. As you read the history, you think they’re going to have mercy on him. They’re going to feel sorry for him. They’re going to say, “He rescued this thief-catcher.” You think they’d be merciful, but they’re not at all. They condemned him, and he was taken to his execution one day after he was judged. And it went from bad to worse. As they put him on the fire, the Martyrs Mirror account tells of a wind that was blowing. The wind blew the fire away from the upper part of his body, so he was burning in excruciating pain, but the wind kept the fire from consuming him. Many in his position would have died quickly from the smoke. He was screaming, and the Martyrs Mirror account records that seventy times over, they heard him cry out, “Oh my Lord, my God.” Seventy times. This was a hard death. Until finally the bailiff from the castle saw it and ordered, “Make this a quick death,” and put an end to the misery. You were talking about them not having mercy. This was law, and he had broken the law. The thief-catcher, if he had freed him, would also have been breaking the law. He would have been a traitor. What struck me was the tragedy of it: a man does something he should have done. He saved a person’s life. He could have turned and run, but he did what was right. And the other man, the one saved from death in the water, would have liked to free him, but his officer told him to hold Willems. You have to wonder what was going on in both of their minds. But this illustrates, I think, perfectly the kind of world we live in. It’s a world that’s tragic because of the fall. And even when you turn to God, there’s still tragedy. I think there was tragedy both for Willems and for the man he saved. We also know Dirk was from this town. In the old etching there is an estimate of where he lived. You can see this church, you can see the castle, and you can see roughly where Dirk lived. A small town, a small village. There’s a lot built into that turning back that is very human, very emotional. History doesn’t really tell us what happened to the thief-catcher he pulled from the ice. It leaves us with a bit of mystery, and reflection: what happened to his story, and how would that have affected his life? You would never forget something like that. 44:20 | What to Expect from This Series On this series, sometimes when we need to go deeper, or explain something that isn’t location-specific, we’ll do what we call cafe chats, where we can dig further into certain pieces. We want to start that here, in this first episode, to outline what viewers can expect. One of the things we’re emphasizing with this documentary series is going to the places where it happened. What can people expect as they go through the series? What all will we cover? Well, the movement started in Zurich, and that is where we will start. We will see how a group of young men became attached to what the Scriptures said and eventually started this movement. The third episode, the Michael Sattler episode, I’m really looking forward to. It’s based on the life of Michael Sattler, and I’ve never been to this monastery, so we will have the opportunity to visit the monastery where he had his conversion, and where the peasant revolt rises and he responds to it. From there we follow him to Strasbourg, and then to Schleitheim. That episode will have a lot of great locations. Then we’ll go to Rattenberg and dig into Pilgram Marpeck, a figure we don’t talk about very often, and what was happening in the Tyrol. That moves us into Austria. And from there we go to the Hutterites. We see how the movement spreads north and east, and how one particular group becomes communitarian. They own everything together, and they actually become very successful, prosperous, and mission-minded. Then we go on to Strasbourg, and to the places where Melchior Hoffman comes in. The movement was starting to head north, and we spend time there looking at the different places, including the prison where he was held. From Hoffman we trace the story as it moves up north. After that comes religion and violence, with two focuses. One is the Peasant Revolt, which started before the Anabaptist movement and lasted until after the movement began. The other is Münster, where we see a movement that starts out peacefully getting derailed, and some of the Anabaptists feeling they need to defend themselves. Out of the disaster that is Münster comes a huge figure in the early Anabaptist movement: Menno Simons. At that point we’re up in the Netherlands, and we’ll tell the story of how he enters the movement from being a Catholic priest, and how he leaves that behind. We filmed in the church where he had been a priest before he became an Anabaptist. After that is church and persecution: the remarkable places the church met, from barns to hidden churches to caves. And then our last episode is about the Dutch experience, at least in part. It’s interesting: they had many divisions among themselves, but we see their attempts to unite, their experience of becoming wealthy and accepted in society, and the effects of that on them as a people. This is a big story with a wide cast of characters. So many fascinating people, empires rising and falling, kings and magistrates and church officials persecuting these new radicals, these early Anabaptists. There are many pieces to this story, and we want to do it justice and give it the time it needs to be told. So this is a fairly long series. If you’re watching and think we’ve missed something, wait: we may cover it later, because there is so much material we want to communicate. As we sit here in Europe and think back 500 years, things looked very different. What happened? 48:27 | Next Episode: Zurich In this ten-part series we ask one haunting question: why did Dirk Willems turn back? In the next episode we go to Zurich, 500 years ago, where the first adult baptisms take place in secret. These believers broke from the state church at great risk to their lives. What did they believe that was so disruptive that the state church ordered their imprisonment and execution? Next Episode The Choice to Believe – Episode 02

title: The Choice to Believe
description: Anabaptists Defied Zurich’s City Council and Baptized Each Other. The Church Struck Back
text: Episode 02      |    Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz, George Blaurock The Choice to Believe Anabaptists Defied Zurich’s City Council and Baptized Each Other. The Church Struck Back 48 min 1519 – 1527 Zurich, Switzerland; Vienna, Austria; Zollikon, Switzerland About This Episode The year is 1525. The place is Zurich, Switzerland, just up the hill from the Limmat River. A small group of young people, including Conrad Grebel, George Blaurock, and Felix Manz, meet secretly in the upstairs room of a house to make a monumental and illegal decision—so illegal that Felix Manz would die for it in that same Limmat River, within earshot of where they met. Join Dean Taylor, Stephen Russell, and Reagan Schrock as they walk these same streets and lead us through the story. Discover how incredibly personal and risky their decision was to be rebaptized, and how they went from being esteemed students of Zwingli, to outcasts on the run. Anabaptist Origins is a 10-part documentary series produced by Anabaptist Perspectives that tells the story of the first hundred years of the Anabaptist movement. View Episode Credits Here: anabaptistorigins.org/credits/ Read the Transcript 0:00 | Cold Open: A Discouraged Student in Paris It’s January 1519, and a young, discouraged student at the University of Paris sits hunched at his desk. His name was Conrad Grebel, and he lived in this house right behind me, across the street. He’s discouraged because he’s just been expelled from the University for brawling, womanizing, and general disorder. It’s a time of great change. Martin Luther has just nailed his 95 theses to the church door. There are rumblings that the Reformation is making its way into Zurich, Switzerland, which is Conrad Grebel’s home city. It was out of these times of uncertainty that the first band of Anabaptists began to form. Within a few short years, all of its original leaders would be dead. Conrad Grebel dies of the plague. George Blaurock is exiled out of the city and hunted to his death. And Felix Manz is drowned here in Zurich. But out of those beginnings, the Radical Reformation spreads beyond Zurich and quickly across the rest of Europe. 1:20 | Three Young Men in Zurich Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz, and George Blaurock were young men, two of them still in their twenties, shaped by the fierce Scriptural teaching of Ulrich Zwingli. They had been some of his most devoted students, but in the winter of 1525 they would go further than their teacher was willing to go. With a simple act of water and confession, they baptized one another as believing adults, and in doing so became outlaws and the founders of Swiss Anabaptism. Their story unfolded against the backdrop of a cracking empire. Luther’s break with the Roman Catholic Church had shaken ancient foundations, and across the German lands, peasants were reaching for their weapons in revolt. 2:01 | Vienna: The Death of Maximilian So we’ve been talking about Conrad Grebel, and he’s from Switzerland, in Zurich specifically. He’s also studying at the University of Paris. While he’s there, he hears about a very significant event, which is the death of the emperor Maximilian. And now we’re here in Vienna, Austria. So we’re way east of where Conrad Grebel would have lived, way east of Paris. But at the time, the Holy Roman Empire, the Habsburg Empire, with Maximilian as its emperor, is this massive, sprawling empire. And we’re right here. This is the palace complex of that. Mr. Russell, do you want to give us a little more context on that, and why we should care about it? How does that affect Conrad Grebel’s story, and really the context around what is shaping up there in Zurich with the Radical Reformation? Well, we’ve already talked a little bit about Maximilian. He did die when Conrad Grebel was at the University of Paris. Soon after the emperor died, Conrad Grebel’s father told him to come back home. But it’s interesting just to get a sense of how important the Holy Roman Empire was. When Maximilian died, the grandson of Maximilian was elected. And he was very young. He was 19. This is Charles V. And so this is where you really get a large empire, because he was also ruler of Spain, which gave him all of the colonies Spain had in the New World. So there was a lot of wealth coming in, and a lot of territory under his command. 3:42 | Zurich and the State Church During these times of change across the empire, the Reformation came to Conrad Grebel’s home city of Zurich, Switzerland. And Ulrich Zwingli, the people’s priest in Zurich, began pushing for changes in the church. Just a second ago we heard some bells chiming across the river as we’re here in Zurich. You mentioned how that was the state church, but all the state churches here are Protestant. Was it always that way? Give us a backdrop of what was going on here with the Reformation. We’re here with the statue of Zwingli. Give us some of the big picture. The Catholic Church became the state church at the end of the 300s. So from that point on, you’ve always had a state church in Europe. The Protestant Reformation broke that up. Not that people stopped being part of the state church, but now there’s the Catholic state church and several Protestant state churches. We’re in Zurich because this is the epicenter of the Swiss Protestant Reformation, but also of our movement. People started reading the New Testament and becoming dissatisfied with the state of the church. There was a lot of corruption. It wasn’t completely corrupt, but there was a lot of corruption. And so one of the reasons Zwingli was invited to come here was because he was recognized as an evangelical preacher. 5:02 | Where Zwingli Landed This is supposedly where he landed. You have a canal right here, the river going through Zurich. And what was this 500 years ago and more? Zwingli gets off a boat, supposedly sets foot right here. First place, right here. How about that? And then he’s going to preach at the church that is way up there. That’s the Grossmünster. The interesting thing is he was reading Erasmus’s Greek New Testament and his commentaries. So while he was preaching at the pilgrimage church, he was already changing his understanding. He was already essentially a Protestant when he came here. And then that becomes the spark that spreads from here, and you have the Swiss Reformation. 5:47 | Preaching Straight Through the Bible The other thing you have coming up, of course, is the Word of God being put out. You’ve got the liturgical preaching that had been going on for hundreds of years. Zwingli takes the Bible and starts reading through Matthew. He even makes it a rule: I’m not going to go to the pulpit unless I am fulfilling this. So they’re actually taking the Bible and putting it into practice and saying, this is the Word of God. And that changed everything. The Catholic Church had a liturgical calendar and a lectionary. A lectionary told you what to read that day from Scripture, and supposedly you would preach from it, at least if you were capable of preaching. Zwingli followed Erasmus. Erasmus had a big commentary on Matthew, and he also did a commentary on Acts. And so the first day that Zwingli preached, which was not a Sunday, he read Matthew 1 and started preaching, and everybody knew that’s not the right reading. And then he said, and I’m going to read chapter 2 tomorrow and talk about that. And it just got people coming to the church like crazy. After he was done with Matthew, he went to Acts. Like I said, Erasmus focused on those two to show how Jesus intended the church to be formed, and then the examples given in the book of Acts. He hoped the preaching would get all of the people on board, including the government. There’s something that can be said for what he did. I don’t agree with it, but there’s something that can be said for what he was trying to do. 7:13 | Twelve Hundred Years of State Church A lot of this stuff seems so obvious to us. Why did they have a state church? Why didn’t they let people choose for themselves? But if you think back, this had been the case since the late 300s. So we’re talking about 1,200 years of people experiencing the church through the state church, with the church and the state tied together. And so when Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz and George Blaurock said this isn’t right, that people should choose consciously as adults that they want to be part of the church, that was scary. It was terribly scary, because it seemed like the church and the state worked together to hold society together. And if you let people choose whether they’re going to be part of this church, will that have an effect on the state? 8:04 | The Sword and the Bible That drills into another point here, the gripes, I guess you could say, that the first Anabaptists had with Zwingli. Grebel says something to the effect of Rome and Jerusalem getting mixed up. He didn’t like what he saw Zwingli doing with the state church and religion. And that’s where you start seeing some of these splits. Can you talk to me a bit about that? What does Zwingli do in that situation with the whole state church question, because he doesn’t necessarily change the situation. No. When you look at the core of what made them different: they’re following with him, they’re studying the Bible, they’re getting charged up, they’re really growing. But then he keeps making his decisions based upon the courts here. He actually resigned from being the people’s priest. But then he stayed within the politics here in Zurich, and as a minister and a pastor and part of that, that was how he was going to bring in reform. The early Anabaptists were saying, should we be looking to the state to make these decisions? I would like to make a remark. He’s got the Bible there on top of the sword. The sword is the state, and the state undergirds the church, but the church undergirded the state as well. This is the symbol of the sword and the Bible together, which so much of all of these episodes are going to be talking about: how that was a trouble, and the disasters that it made. One of the reasons the church was so corrupted in 1500 is that for 1,200 years the church and state had been working together. So political power was a huge thing for the Catholic Church, but it’s not any less for the Protestant Church either. And the term they use, the Magisterial Reformation, means they’re using the magistrates. It’s within the established magistrates that they’re doing this. That’s why we have the Magisterial Reformation. And when you think of our darkest moments in Christianity, it’s usually when these two are mixed together. 10:05 | Jacob Grebel and the French Money So Conrad Grebel’s time in Paris is finishing. Zwingli is starting to do some things here in Zurich. Grebel comes back to Zurich at this point. Give me a little more context. What’s going on here? While Conrad was being not a good guy in Paris, and it wasn’t working out very well, this is when Zwingli is really showing himself well here. And he hears about the womanizing, he hears about the fights, and he’s very humiliated by it. He’s actually worried that Conrad is hurting not only the name of his own family, but Zurich itself. And what’s happening right now is some pretty big tensions with everything in Europe, with the Empire and the election of Charles V. Francis I of France loved to use his money, and he had lots of money, to buy friendships. I’ll buy you this, I’ll buy you that. And one of the people who took money from him was Conrad’s father, for the scholarship in Paris. So he takes the money, and it ends up being a terrible thing. Because later in his life, when all the turmoil is happening, around 1526, they arrest Jacob, bring him in here, and try him for treason for taking that money from Francis of France. And they execute him by beheading right here. There was already trouble. Conrad had married below his status, and it was a scandal to his family. So she’s trying to make it work with him being this missionary and this apostle. Now Jacob dies, and it’s a pretty hard time in the home. The point being, just laying the context of what’s going on, how these early beginnings for the Anabaptist movement come together in Conrad Grebel. You can read about his life, but there are all these layers of context around it. Francis I of France, and the money that’s being exchanged, and how Conrad Grebel’s father Jacob Grebel is on the city council, which is right here in the Rathaus. There are a lot of layers going on here, and just what a chaotic time it was to live. Jacob Grebel is executed. The first Anabaptist martyrs are being killed. There’s a lot happening. It must have been a difficult time to be alive. 12:31 | Who Was Conrad Grebel? So tell me about this guy named Conrad Grebel. Here we are at Conrad Grebel’s house in Zurich. This is not a guy who was born ultra-religious. He keeps trying to get into college, keeps coming out of it. He ends up in Paris, and when he’s in Paris he’s kind of a flop. Not a flop academically, just getting into trouble. He gets into drunkenness, he’s apparently womanizing, and by the end of that he gets letters back telling him, it’s time for you to come home. What I think is pretty interesting is that soon after he came back, he got into the circle of other young men who were studying with Zwingli. And at first the point wasn’t, or at least Zwingli didn’t make it the point, that we’re going to study the Greek New Testament. In fact, they started with Plato’s writings. And we saw that very thing today. Yes, we saw Zwingli’s personal copy of Plato’s Republic. It says “This belongs to Zwingli” on the front. And they go from Plato and the classics to the New Testament. And then Zwingli had them translate into more or less standard German, and then into the local dialect. Zwingli, before the split, was planning on starting what we would call a seminary. He wanted both of those men to teach, one to teach Greek and one to teach Hebrew. I don’t remember which was which. Because of their falling out, that didn’t happen. But that says something about what he thought of them. He respected them. He thought they were good students, and they must have been, if he was thinking about asking them to teach Hebrew and Greek. One of the things that gets me too is when you read his letters. Here’s this foolish young man, all his parties, messed up and everything. But then, in 1522, the letters change. He’s suddenly talking about the things of God, the kingdom of God. He gets married, against his parents’ wishes, and the parents never really fully reconciled to that. He eventually goes off doing mission work. And after that happens, his wife actually comes back to the state church. But the thing is, they never really accepted her, and so that was hard. They have a couple of children, and they’re living here with the dynamics of the in-laws and all of that. But he feels this calling. He’s a church planter. He’s one of the leaders of this whole movement now. And he leaves from here and never comes back. Probably thinking, I’ll be back soon. And he walks into the pages of history and vanishes. We don’t really know what happens after that. He dies of the plague, as far as we can tell. But even that, we don’t know where exactly he died. 15:31 | The Letters to Vadian So, pondering: what do you think? What are the things about his theology, about his zeal, that connect with today’s message? I think of the quote that you use a lot, from that letter he’s writing to his mentor. I see this in Scripture, and that’s what it has to come back to. That is the decision point between Grebel and his group and Zwingli, when they believe: Zwingli, you’re just listening to the council. You should be listening to God’s Word. And that is such an important legacy that sticks with us to this day. What is Scripture calling us to? So right here, writing a letter to Vadian, he says: “I believe the Word of God without complicated interpretation. And out of this belief, I speak. May God give you the mercy to submit to his Word without reservation and obey it. Otherwise, things probably don’t stand as well with us as we might hope. The way is narrow.” And then in his final letter, at least his final letter to Vadian, he has this: “The teaching of the Lord has been given for the purpose of being put into practice.” In there he said something about how, if you don’t take the same route I do, our relationship will not be as close. This was his brother-in-law. 16:52 | Flawed Men and a Lasting Legacy That’s the one piece I’m starting to see as we’re going around to these different sites: how close everything is. It’s like, we were just down at the river where Felix Manz was drowned, and right over here is the Grossmünster, and right over here is where the city council met to have those disputations and figure out what they were going to do. And right here is Conrad Grebel’s house, and Felix Manz is right down the road. If somebody was screaming at the river, you’d probably hear it here. It really makes you think about how disruptive this could have been at the level of the functioning of society, in a small-town environment. You’re talking about an entire Europe that’s persecuting people and killing them and going to war and making a mockery out of the Word of God. And finally we’ve got the words of Jesus, and they’re saying, why are we in this whole huge system of church and state, and this view of the church, which is just wrong? I think that’s an important piece to add here. We want to tell that story and how important it is for us today, while also acknowledging these were humans. They were flawed. Those are all important pieces of the story. I think it’s important for us to sit with those stories and wrestle with them, and not just say they’re the greatest people to ever live. They were human, trying to do the best they could with the information they were learning. And so much of this is fresh. It’s like learning it for the first time. That’s how I try to think about it. So, taking up his challenge, taking his letter and applying it to us: do the next generations believe the Word of God without a complicated interpretation? And out of that, do we speak and live our lives, because the way is narrow? And do we take up the words of Jesus and put them into practice? I think those two bedrocks of early Anabaptism that came right out of here can still give a legacy to last for centuries to come. 18:48 | The Rathaus and the Disputations Zwingli began having Bible studies with a small group of students, including Conrad Grebel and Felix Manz. What they were reading was beginning to clash with what they saw around them: the Mass, infant baptism, and the church’s entanglement with civic power. Trouble was brewing as Zwingli took his case to the city council, pushing for the government’s backing of these new ideas. This led to a series of disputations, with the city council trying to decide what to do with these radical new concepts. Walking up to the Rathaus. What about this building specifically is important to where we are in the story with Zwingli and the Reformation that’s happening here in Zurich? This is the seat of government. So whatever would happen with government, the city council met here and made laws. It’s the center of the government, not just for the city but for the whole canton of Zurich. So all the things that happened, like when they were having their disputations, and when they were deciding on executing someone. Now, there was a wooden building here in those days. This one’s been replaced, but this is still the spot. And this is the area where executions took place and people would have gathered. You mentioned disputations. Tell me what a disputation was, and why was Zwingli doing a bunch of them? A disputation would be where you have a particular issue, and you try to discuss it and come to a decision. This is what we should do, or believe, about this particular thing. After Zwingli resigned and was chosen by the city council still to be the people’s priest, but now under their authority, under the civil authority, they had a disputation. They invited all of the Catholic priests, because this was still Catholic. They invited all the priests here, and they wanted to convince them that things were going to change. And the bishop sent in a representative, but it was only to tell them: this is illegal. I didn’t allow this. So this counts for nothing. And all of that’s happening right here? Yes, in the old wooden building. The city council is the judge. So they make the decision about who’s right. Is the bishop’s representative right, or is Zwingli right? Well, Zwingli was right. So they asked him to keep on preaching as he had been preaching. And then in October, Zwingli thought the preaching had gone on long enough and the people, he hoped, would be with him. And so they had another disputation, and they were trying to figure out about various Catholic practices: the Mass, purgatory, images, things like that. They discussed all this and decided the Mass is not really the way we should worship. They got to the end of the first day and announced what they were going to talk about the next day. But these proto-Anabaptists, these young men who were soon going to be Anabaptists, objected. When are we going to end the Mass? Because we just decided it’s not proper. It’s not scriptural. Yes, it’s not scriptural. And so Zwingli said, “My lords, the council, will decide when.” And this is where the tension starts, because Zwingli would say, we did agree, but the council will decide the speed. And these young men said, well, we decided it’s unscriptural, so we should move ahead. And Zwingli agreed that it was unscriptural. And so it goes from being a Bible study in your church with the minister, Zwingli in this case, to: okay, now let’s come over to the city council and decide at a government level whether we can do this. And they were on board until it went too slow. In fact, at one point Grebel suggested to Zwingli that they organize a political party, take over the council, and move things along. He decided later that Zwingli didn’t want to do it. And he decided, no, that church and state thing is really not what we want. 22:48 | Grebel Withdraws What was Grebel’s response when Zwingli said, we’re going to let the council decide the pace? One of the things he did was write to Vadian, who is his brother-in-law. He feels that the ones we thought were God’s servants have bound the Word. And it’s so crystal clear. And he says, I can’t submit to this. He felt betrayed. And he felt the gospel was betrayed, because we’re supposed to be out there telling people that you have to hear the gospel, you have to see your condition, and you have to repent. After the disputation where Zwingli said, “My lords, the council, will decide how fast this thing goes,” basically those people who were going to become Anabaptists withdrew. They started doing their own thing. They started writing Bible studies and doing Bible studies with the people. And so basically all of 1524 was these young men working to promote their understanding of the Reformation. So that’s what’s happening in 1524. And toward the end of that, Manz wants to try one more time. He requests another disputation to try to show that infant baptism is not right. And so they do have another. The third disputation is in January of 1525. Basically they are just told that you’re wrong and that you have to have your children baptized. These are young men and women, so they’re starting to have children, and they’re not baptizing them. It is law to baptize your children. And it gets really personal for Conrad Grebel. Conrad Grebel has a daughter, a week or two before that council. So council members bring them in and basically say, you have to do this. You have to submit. And if you’re not a citizen of Zurich, you’ve got to leave. There were others, but the three main leaders are probably Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz, and George Blaurock. But George Blaurock is not a Zuricher. It looks like Michael Sattler made it to some of these. It looks like Hubmaier made it to some of these. And then they left, or would have been told to get out of town. So that becomes the decision point, that last council in January of 1525. Look, the council members are saying, you have to baptize your infants. If you don’t. Within eight days. Within eight days, okay. So there’s a timeline on this. So this is why the baptisms are going to happen, because of the state saying you’re wrong, you have to submit. And then these men and women are trying to figure out what they should do. 25:46 | January 21, 1525 In mid-January, the air in Zurich grew tense. After a public debate on baptism, the city council ruled that every unbaptized child in the canton was to be baptized within eight days, and any parent who refused would be banished. Three days later, the council tightened its grip, silencing Grebel and Manz, shutting down their Bible meetings, and ordering their supporters from outside Zurich to leave the territory. That very night, January 21st, 1525, a small band slipped into the house of Felix Manz’s mother, a short walk from the Grossmünster church where they had once studied beside Zwingli. They prayed, they read Scripture, then George Blaurock asked Conrad Grebel to baptize him as a believing adult. Then the rest of the group took the dangerous step of baptizing one another as believers. It was a simple act, water and confession in a private house, but it reshaped the Reformation. By March the next year, Zurich had issued a new mandate. Rebaptism was now punishable by death. But the course was already set. 26:53 | The Hutterian Chronicle Account Here’s the account written in the Hutterian Chronicles, which is where we have the story from. It says this: “And it came to pass that they were together with one accord at the house of the mother of Felix Manz in Zurich, lamenting before God with great prayer that he would teach them the right path, for they were deeply moved in their hearts. And when fear of God pressed them, so that they dared not wait longer, George of the house of Jacob Blaurock stood up and asked Conrad Grebel to baptize him with the true Christian baptism upon his faith and knowledge. And when he knelt down with such a request and desire, Conrad baptized him, since at the time there had been no ordained ministers to perform such work. After that, the others asked George to baptize them, which he did. In this way they gave themselves to the name of the Lord in the high fear of God. They confirmed one another for the service of the gospel,” notice, right from the beginning, “and they began to teach and hold the faith.” And then this last statement: “This was the beginning of separation from the world and of the assembling of those who were willing to live their lives according to the teachings of Christ and obey his commandments.” To me, that sounds like: we’re here because the state is putting pressure on us to baptize our children. And then the Spirit moves. So I really think this was not the plan. Now, this is my take on what they said beforehand and during this. I think the main question they would have been asking was, we don’t want to baptize our children, so should we leave? What should we do? Well, when Blaurock said, baptize me on the confession of my faith, that sealed it, and it started a completely different thing. They were asking for their children to be left alone so that they could decide to be baptized or not. The point being, as soon as that act of baptism is done, you have reached a decision point. At that point, okay, this has happened. And we’ve very clearly said, we’re going this direction. Blaurock was baptized by Grebel, the obvious leader of the movement. And it says there was no ordained church leader. What I want us to notice is that the Anabaptists were sometimes accused of being anarchists. But if you read Schleitheim, if you read Dordrecht, if you read what they do when they organize: one of the things Schleitheim says is that as soon as a minister is either driven away by the state or executed, choose another one right away. They were very clear that there needs to be organization. It shows up in Schleitheim, but Schleitheim is two years later. And that might have been in there because they saw the problems when there were individualistic Anabaptists at first. What’s interesting also is that Blaurock was a priest. Correct me if I’m wrong. No, he was a priest. A really wild one. This was so interesting. You have the priest that’s there, and he says, someone else baptize me. That turns things different from what we’re used to seeing. Another aspect of that was that Luther had already taught the priesthood of the believers. They knew that. These people here knew that. And so Blaurock may have been the ordained priest, but they knew that if they really are followers of Jesus, they’re all priests. So the possibility of any one of them baptizing wasn’t out of the question. But they also still wanted to be organized, to be respectful, orderly. So I’m curious. I’m seeing there’s a fountain right there. Would there have been a well? Did you go out and get your pail of water? Theoretically, could this have been where they actually scooped the water up? Or am I speculating too much? Oh, it probably is, because where else is a water source here? But it does say that it happened in the room upstairs. You can imagine: we need some water to do this baptism, and coming down and getting a pitcher of water and taking it up. What was life like for them living here? And what was day-to-day life like after this moment in time happens? What did that look like? We can’t walk this one back. You’ve got to walk forward now in faith. 31:19 | Zollikon: The First Congregation So the baptisms occurred in Zurich on January 21. But just weeks after that happened, the authorities cracked down on adult baptism, and the church had to go underground. And it was right here, right here in Zollikon, that the first church came to life. Here they met and worked out the teachings they had talked about and learned about and tried to put into practice: how they immediately wanted to start having communion, how they started sharing and baptizing. And through their preaching and their passion, a revival broke out. You can just kind of feel it, even by reading the details of how they gathered here, the radical young things that were happening. It sounds like with George Blaurock coming here, they’re breaking into communion, and then the next day they’re starting to baptize people. They’re figuring out the details of the whole thing. And this concept of being a gathered community of discipled believers, apart from the state church, a city in the kingdom of God, was now just being able to come to life. And this would have started in January. But as you said, the authorities cracked down very hard. And so really, the church here only lasted as an individual congregation until about the end of April. And then people had to scatter. The baptisms are on January 21st, like you just said. And then they come over to here, which is a short walk, actually. And if I’m remembering right, they’re already starting to do baptisms and gatherings within a couple of days of that first baptism back in Zurich. Within a couple of weeks, we ended up with over 200 believers from the evangelism in this town. Remember, it’s a crime. It’s a crime. They’ve made it clear. No adult baptisms. It was easier to enforce their mandate in the city, that there aren’t going to be any Anabaptists there. But it’s out here in the countryside where they had trouble. Yes, during those months the people would get arrested and freed and arrested again. And eventually most of them said, okay, I’ll go back to the state church. And basically the church then has to go underground. It goes into caves. It goes into the fields. It goes into barns and hiding places. And they realize they can’t just be here in homes like this. Through that scattering, the message spreads incredibly quickly, and very broad and wide. We’ll see that as we keep going through this series and go to a lot of these different places. They end up at far-flung corners of all kinds of places out of this. 34:01 | Sympathizers and the True Hearted Well, we talked to the pastor at the Grossmünster, and one of the things he mentioned was that an awful lot of the people didn’t become Anabaptists, but they supported them. And once again, that fits a little bit with the fact that the city of Zurich had the rest of the canton sort of under their thumb. People didn’t like that. And so even if you didn’t have a lot of Anabaptists here, you usually had a lot of sympathizers. They were sometimes called half-Anabaptists, or there was another term. What was the other term? True hearted. Yes, the true hearted. So the interesting thing is, even if you didn’t become an Anabaptist, you often said, well, that’s my neighbor. And I’m not going to turn him in to the state. We don’t know what went on in their minds. But look, Zwingli and the people in Zurich just rebelled against the Catholic Church. And so there might also have been this attitude of, why do we have to listen to them? I don’t know for sure. Along with the pressure the city put on the people out in the country, there could have just been a recognition that there’s something not quite right here. If it’s okay for Zurich to break away from the Catholic Church, why can’t these people who want to meet do that? The rapidity, how rapidly the message came when people would come in and preach, and the response people had to that. People couldn’t understand it. They literally thought there must be something weird going on. How can people change their whole way of life at the preaching of this message so quickly? So there was something inside there that was wanting and waiting for something. This is the place they worked out the congregational order, where they talked about meeting three or four times a week. They had frequent communion. They would share a common pot, so that where there were needs, they would help each other out. And from all those things, from here, it went all over the world. 36:04 | Punishable by Drowning We’ve laid some groundwork at this particular spot, which is hugely significant for the Anabaptist origin story, especially that last council where they’re saying, you have to do infant baptism. That’s the split moment where it’s like, okay, we have to make a decision. And now, with everything happening in Zollikon and all the people starting to really push this, the government struck back. They actually made a mandate and put a sentence to it: anyone who’s doing these adult baptisms, punishable by drowning. Which is really crazy. You think, this is a group of people who just came out of persecution from the Roman Catholic system because of the Reformation. Now they’re still going back and using the state church system to persecute people they disagree with. But the prisons couldn’t hold them. They would arrest them, and then miraculously a door would be left open and they would escape from prison. There was a tower in the middle where they would put the prisoners. So they escaped from prison. And that was crazy. I think no one would fault them if we read in our textbooks, “and then they went and hid out for six months until the heat was off.” No. They literally go right back to preaching. That is at the core of Anabaptism: that you love everyone. And that means you tell them the gospel. 37:30 | Where the Word Anabaptist Comes From Where does the term Anabaptist come into the story? What does that word even mean? Who came up with it? It’s a loaded word. The word Anabaptism, which literally means rebaptizers, is not just a label. It’s a death sentence. By using this term, when the reformers used it, they were invoking ancient imperial laws that spelled out that it was against the law to do any kind of rebaptizing. And so they were using these to bring that charge against them. These kinds of charges go way back. Emperors such as Justinian I and Theodosius I made these laws about Christianity, combining the church and the state in a very destructive way, in my opinion. And this is a long time ago we’re talking about. This is a long time ago. With Theodosius you’re talking at the end of the 4th century, the late 300s, and with Justinian you’re coming to the end of the 500s. But still, these men brought these kinds of church and state laws and codified things that made any kind of dissent like this a capital offense. And because of that, they paved the way for many centuries of this kind of killing, this kind of punishment for religious dissent. This is a sign of how closely church and state were operating together, because the first codification of Roman law includes church law. The accusation “Anabaptist” comes from way back, even before Theodosius, where church and state were close together and the Donatists were causing problems. The Donatists would rebaptize the Catholics who came to them. And so it was made a law that a person who rebaptized would be executed. And so that’s what the city council in Zurich, or whatever entity, is pulling back to, and saying, we’re going to use that to hold you. The word is loaded with that. Exactly. And so these reformers weren’t breaking from the past with this whole concept of church and state and the empire all together. They were channeling it. So here is this term which has now followed us to this day, but it was a loaded word in their day. 39:52 | Felix Manz and the Letter from Chur So these guys keep getting thrown into prison. They’re thrown in prison in Zollikon and in Zurich. They’re thrown in the prison tower in Zurich in the middle of the river multiple times. That tower is not there anymore, so we’re in a different medieval prison tower. I’ve got some letters, particularly looking at Felix Manz. On the far eastern side of Switzerland, in the little town of Chur, he begins to go preaching right on the street. And we literally have this letter that the city of Chur wrote to Zurich, talking about how they’re very upset about this guy named Felix Manz, dated July 13th, 1525. January 21st, 1525 is the first baptism. Now he’s already on the other side of the country preaching, captured, escaped, preaching again. And now they’re writing this letter. “For a long time we have had among us one who calls himself Felix Manz. The same has created much trouble and discord among our people by baptizing old people and corner preaching.” Baptizing old people?
