It’s kind of humorous language to think of now, but at that time you didn’t baptize anyone other than a baby. Yes, you’re only baptizing babies. “To such an extent that we ordered him to leave the city.” But he came back. “After this, he returned and did as before, disregarding the public proclamation in the church forbidding adult baptism on penalty of death, loss of honor, and loss of property. Therefore we arrested him and held him for a few days.” But, now, city of Zurich, “but because he is an obstinate and recalcitrant person, we released him from prison. And because he is one of yours, we have sent him to you with the friendly request that you look after him and keep him in your territory, so that we may be rid of him and our people remain quiet, and that in case of his return we are not compelled to take severe measures against him.” So imagine he goes back in chains to Zurich with this letter. Zwingli’s getting hold of this letter. They’re thinking, oh wow, now our reputation. You can imagine a lot of dynamics going through all of that. 42:13 | The Trial and the Sentence When he gets back to Zurich, he goes back to preaching again. And eventually they’ve had enough. And so they arrest him, try him, and then it’s the remarkable thing. We’re already seeing that Zwingli is using different coercion measures and this type of thing. But now, for one of the Reformed churches to actually encourage this, though of course not formally, and this was the connection between the church and the state. But to encourage it: we’ve had enough. We can’t change his mind theologically, or in disputes or debates. We’re going to kill him. And that brings back all of that medieval type of thing, where the church uses the power of the sword. And the execution proclamation says a lot about the theology of the early Anabaptists and the things he was tried for. So let’s read that. This was finally read out when he was going to be executed. “Because contrary to Christian order and custom, he had become involved in Anabaptism.” Again, we use that term so frequently now, but this was using those Justinian codes against him. This is his charge. “He had accepted it, taught others, and become a leader and beginner of these things, because he has confessed having said that he wanted to gather those who wanted to accept Christ and follow him.” That’s a charge. “And unite himself with them through baptism, and let the rest live according to their faith, so that he and his followers separated themselves from the Christian church and were about to raise up and prepare a sect of their own under the guise of a Christian meeting in church. And because he has condemned capital punishment. But since such doctrine is harmful to the unified usage of all Christendom, and leads to offense, insurrection, and sedition against the government, to the shattering of the common peace, brotherly love, and civil cooperation, and to all evil. Manz shall be delivered to the executioner, who shall tie his hands, put him into a boat, take him to the lower hut,” that’s the fishing hut we see in the ancient paintings, “there strip his bound hands down over his knees, place a stick between his knees and arms, and there push him into the water and let him perish in the water. Thereby he shall have atoned to the law and justice, and his properties shall then be confiscated by my lords.” And then there we are. We can go right out there to the plaque, to where this happened. It’s like, wait, he’s getting killed for theological beliefs and for following Christ. But that was considered: you’re a destabilizing force in society, because church and state are intertwined. Yes, so what you believe theologically could actually be a state charge against you. 45:25 | The Plaque on the Limmat So this is the plaque. Unless churches actually repent of their theology, similar circumstances in history have proven that you may go through different phases of good behavior, but if your theology doesn’t change, similar circumstances could actually bring out the same results. To give credit to the Reformed church here, this was a huge public apology and repentance from the Reformed church. They came here with a boat and threw roses, and put up this plaque. What it does is acknowledge the cruelty of the persecution that happened to the Anabaptists here, and they wanted this never to happen again. Mr. Russell, could you read this plaque for us? “Here in the middle of the Limmat River, at a fisher platform, Felix Manz and five further Anabaptists in the Reformed time between the years 1527 and 1532 were drowned here.” And then it says, “Hans Landis was the last Anabaptist here in Zurich to be executed, 1614.” At any time of execution like this, of course, it was totally crowded. Zwingli and the ministers were trying to tell him to repent, to recant. If he would just recant, how great that would have been for everything to work out. So they’re telling him to recant, and he wouldn’t even listen to them. And then the Martyrs Mirror records that his mother says, “Be faithful unto death.” And what’s amazing about her: this was a woman who would have been the mistress of a priest at the Grossmünster, and Felix Manz was an illegitimate child born of that. Think of her whole life, of the shame and everything. Now she has her son, and we saw the baptism site and all that type of thing. And now, be faithful unto death. And so with that, we see that the Martyrs Mirror says he actually sang, “Into thy hands I commit my spirit,” and just resolved to serve God. And he was drowned here in the Limmat River. And that was 1527 when that happened. This was in January. From here, the Schleitheim Confession, the martyrdom of Michael Sattler. This was a big year. And it had a hard start, right here. 47:53 | Next Episode: The Peasants’ War and a Young Monk A lot happened in Zurich, but that was just the beginning. In the next episode, we’ll explore the tensions that emerged between violent revolutions like the Peasants’ War and the Anabaptist radical call to suffer and serve. Caught in the middle of these two worldviews is a young Catholic monk forced to make a decision. His choice will permanently affect the future of the Anabaptist movement. title: Seven Intolerable Truths
description: Michael Sattler & The Schleitheim Confession: The Peaceful Revolution Takes Shape
text: Episode 03      |    Michael Sattler, Schleitheim Confession Seven Intolerable Truths Michael Sattler & The Schleitheim Confession: The Peaceful Revolution Takes Shape 62 min 1525 – 1527 St. Peter’s Monastery, Germany; Strasbourg, France; Schleitheim, Switzerland; Rottenburg, Germany About This Episode Episode three takes you on a journey. Starting at a cathedral in the Black Forest, you will follow the life of Michael Sattler. When the Peasants’ War forced him from the monastery, he began a journey that leads us to the other major focus of this episode: the Schleitheim Confession. In the little town of Schleitheim, Switzerland, early Anabaptist leaders gathered to wrestle through their beliefs. What made them different from the Catholic and Protestant churches around them, and why were they willing to suffer and die for these differences? As a vivid illustration of how revolutionary these ideas were, you will end the episode in a field at Michael Sattler’s memorial. There you will hear the brutal story of his trial and martyrdom, which he suffered because he refused to compromise his beliefs in Scripture. Anabaptist Origins is a 10-part documentary series produced by Anabaptist Perspectives that tells the story of the first hundred years of the Anabaptist movement. View Episode Credits Here: anabaptistorigins.org/credits/ Illustration of Michael and Margaretha Sattler by Jason Landsel, 2019. Used by permission. Find Landsel’s work here: https://www.plough.com/contributors/jason-landsel-en ” Read the Transcript 0:00 | Cold Open: The Prior Who Walked Away St. Peter’s monastery, deep in the Black Forest, was a place that was quiet for centuries. Michael Sattler was a rising scholar here, and also the prior of this monastery. But that quiet was shattered in the spring of 1525, when the Peasants’ Revolt ripped through this village. Michael Sattler left the monastery as this cloister was being overrun. Instead, he chose a more radical path and joined the Swiss Brethren, at a time when the Anabaptists were out of step with both the magistrates and the revolutionaries. He helped forge a new path, one that rejected war, vengeance, and revolt, while also forming discipled, close-knit communities. 1:18 | St. Peter’s Monastery Well, here’s St. Peter’s monastery. I cannot believe we are here. It’s definitely of more substantial size than I expected. Much more beautiful, much more substantial than I ever realized. It’s still hard for me to get my head around Michael Sattler walking this way. And the peasants coming through. Mr. Russell, why don’t you start off by telling us the significance of this building, both in the context here and for the Anabaptist story as well. Okay, this is St. Peter’s monastery in the Black Forest. I’ll tell you a little bit about monasteries first, and then a little bit about why it’s part of our story. Monasteries usually had a lot of land, and in the Middle Ages land was wealth. So they were wealthy, and they usually had peasants who worked their land. The relations weren’t always perfect. But there’s a positive side too. These monasteries took care of the poor. They were the inns of the Middle Ages. If you were traveling, you probably would look for a monastery to stay in. So the monasteries were pretty important in the Middle Ages. They were economically important. They helped the poor. And of course, they taught the Catholic religion. One of the reasons this is important for our story is that in the early 1500s, Michael Sattler was the prior here. That means he basically was the person in charge of running the day-by-day things. Almost like an administrator. An administrator, yes, that’s good. And so he was here, a well-educated man. Later on we’re going to read the Schleitheim Confession, and I think that really says a lot about his education. That was a pretty high position, second in command. But other than that, they were also educated. So this would have been the place where you would have studied and translated and things like that. And this would have been a center. There’s an interesting little quote in the Hutterian Chronicles that mentions the education of all the early Anabaptists, and it particularly mentions Michael Sattler. Speaking of the first Swiss Brethren, and including Sattler, it said they all had a thorough knowledge of German, Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. And of Sattler particularly it said he was a scholar in Hebrew and Latin, with a wide knowledge of the Holy Scriptures, a man who truly loved God. And truly, in the leadership of the early Anabaptists, you see these men and their understanding of the Scriptures really gave a lot to it. I think that’s an important piece, his understanding of Scripture and how much it flows through his writings. And again, we’ll be going to Schleitheim, looking at what they did there, and he was a major part of that story. 4:14 | The Spring of 1525 But tell me a bit about the spring of 1525. This is right after the first baptisms happened in Zurich. Conrad Grebel, George Blaurock, Felix Manz and that group are in hiding for the most part. The first church in Zollikon is starting up. But in the spring of 1525, something really significant happens right here at this monastery while Sattler is here. Tell us about that. Well, a little bit before is when the Peasants’ Revolt started. The peasants in this general area were hearing the gospel, and they felt they weren’t being treated right. They actually overwhelmed the monastery. And we think that’s when Sattler left, because he sympathized with them. He then went to Zurich, got in contact with the Anabaptists, and got baptized. Again, the Hutterian Chronicles mentions that he left here shortly after. In some way they were overrun by the peasants who were here. And it’s interesting: it doesn’t give any direct evidence of violence or of tearing the place apart. They were just upset. They were making their petitions. They were bringing them together and making these twelve articles. And he would have heard that. 5:23 | Between Catholic and Protestant I find in the Swiss, in the South Germans, in the Hutterites, there’s something about this sort of monastic past that seems to be there. It feels different from when you read the Dutch. This may sound strange to some of our listeners, but a big part of the Anabaptist movement and motivation was Catholic medieval piety. And so that’s where your question about the monastic thing comes in. The Anabaptists are sort of in between the Protestants, who were much more willing to throw everything out, and the Catholics, who were trying to keep everything. The Anabaptists were right in the middle. For instance, I’ll give you one example. At this point in time there was a question about which books belong in the Old Testament. There wasn’t any question about the New Testament. As the Reformers looked at and translated the Old Testament, they decided they were only going to keep the books that were in Hebrew. The Catholics and the Orthodox had books that at that time were only available in Greek. Probably most of them had been written in Hebrew originally, but the Jews didn’t look at them as Scripture. So what the Protestants decided was, we’re going to go with what the Jews see as Scripture for the Old Testament. The Catholics held on to those pieces we call the Apocrypha. They said they’re the second law, so they maybe didn’t give them exactly equal weight, but they still are Scripture for Catholics. And guess who else they were Scripture for? I don’t care who it is, if you read Menno or Philips or Sattler. The Hutterian Chronicles, the Ausbund. If it has Scripture in it, you’ll find notations where you’ll say, what is that? Sirach and Wisdom. One other, just in case. The Protestants did not believe in free will. Every person was chosen by God to go to heaven or to go to hell. Catholics did not believe that, and we didn’t either. We believe there is real free will. Sometimes we, wanting to give a quick lesson in a history class, divide these lines way too clearly. It was gray. There’s not this neat Reformation split: Protestant, Catholic, Anabaptist. There were people crying out, we need to bring back faith. You can’t have just empty sacraments. We need this. And there were voices like that. There’s a particular passage from Athanasius where he gives us the closest connection from the early church to the canon. And it’s funny, just like you mentioned, Stephen, he mentions all the books of the Bible, and then he says these are other spiritual books that we should read and understand. But they held them at a slightly different level. That seems to be some sort of middle place between the Protestants and the Catholics. And maybe the Anabaptists were somewhere in there. 8:15 | A Gate So Strait A lot of the Protestants at the beginning would have thought that just this talking of grace and faith would automatically make you holy. The Catholics believed in grace and faith too. But they said, okay, you still need to go through the narrow path. The way is narrow. And there’s going to be a lot of effort in it. The early Anabaptists, particularly the Swiss, got hold of that. There’s one of the Martyrs Mirror quotes that always kind of shocked me: they went through a gate so strait they left some flesh on the post. Flesh in the sense of what you want to leave behind. What you want to leave behind, thank you, yes. But it’s interesting. I think it’s Sebastian Franck in his chronicle who uses the idea. He was talking about the different groups of Anabaptists and referring to the Swiss. There are some that even form a new monasticism, a new rule of St. Benedict. And you don’t know exactly who he’s talking about. But that whole general spirituality just makes me ponder the Swiss. Well, there are others who talk about that, and they are pointing to our ancestors, that we are the new… I think Bullinger was one of these. Yes, right. The Anabaptists are the new monastics. They marry, but they try to live like the monks. So, just for some context: he would have been a huge critic of the Anabaptists, and of the monastery. He would have been Zwingli’s successor in Zurich. So he’s writing that. I didn’t realize that’s a slam. Yes, he’s trying to say this is terrible, and they’re kind of this way. I understand now. 9:42 | Beware the Scribes and the Pharisees Well, it is undeniable that some Catholics would have approached their faith as a works righteousness. It’s undeniable. But it’s also undeniable that there were Catholics who got it. And the Catholics who got it would have agreed with James. I will show you my faith through my works. And faith without works is dead. And the Anabaptists agreed with that. Michael Sattler’s work On the Satisfaction of Christ puts it perfectly. He said, we must beware the scribes and the Pharisees. And it’s interesting. He said the Pharisees are how we were in our old way. There we tried to earn our salvation through works, and doing ceremonies, and doing pilgrimages, and this type of thing. We must beware of the Pharisees. But he said we must also be aware of the scribes. The scribes write beautiful things, and they speak beautiful things, but their lives do not show it. And so find the middle path. Beware the scribes and the Pharisees. It’s a beautiful quote that brings the Reformation and the Catholic together in Michael Sattler. And having the context of where he’s coming from, as prior of a substantial institution, he has a lot of history, a lot of understanding, that we sometimes miss. Oh, that’s really cool. The bells are starting to ring. That’s amazing. About 500 years ago, right at 500 years, the Peasants’ War came through here. Michael Sattler would have heard those ringing bells. And how much has changed, but also how much has stayed the same. It’s still here. And the movement that Sattler was so instrumental in is still here as well. There’s something special about that. Really is. 11:23 | Luther, Faith, and Works Luther tried to win his salvation in the monastery, and it drove him crazy. But when he left, he said that you are saved by faith alone. And it doesn’t say that in the Scriptures anywhere, and he was always challenged on that. I just read the other day one of his statements, where he said, if you match faith and works at all, it’s not faith. It’s not saving faith. That’s how strong he was. You only need faith. And if you bring them together, you’re going down the wrong route. And that’s why Luther wanted to take James out of the New Testament. He wanted to get rid of the book of James, because it says we are saved by faith and works. Now, he thought his theology would automatically produce this righteous life. He thought that would happen. It didn’t. And he even says, and Bender brings this up, that even at the end of his life the plan didn’t work. What it did produce was a sort of sloppy theology that he himself eventually had to recognize. And Luther is, in a lot of ways, reacting against what he was experiencing in a monastery situation like this. It was a tense situation, because the people here, if they weren’t Anabaptists, still liked the Anabaptists. Sympathetic. Yes. Even the buildup of the drama in the area was a lot. When they moved him from Horb to here, it was with 24 horsemen. And then the Count here was worrying about a revolt, so he added 56 additional soldiers to go along with it. Imagine Michael Sattler and his wife and at least 13 others, with 24 horses and 56 soldiers. That’s quite a thing coming down the street. And I’m just thinking about the contrast. Here we are, it’s a nice beautiful summer day, there’s a cafe here now, it’s a nice square, people are going about their lives. But back then, almost 500 years from when we’re recording this, times were pretty different, at least in that particular situation. You can imagine that procession coming up that street, which I’m sure was here at the time. That would have been quite the spectacle, and also: whoa, something really serious is happening here. And we’re pretty far removed from that. It’s a little hard for me to get my head around, the contrast between that and what we’re experiencing right now. 49:57 | The Charges So the court here is epic in our Anabaptist history, in the way he was charged and that kind of thing. So I took the records here to discuss them a little back and forth. The date was May 17th, 1527. On the bench was Michael Sattler and his wife Margaretha and about 13, at least 13, others. So you can imagine, in a building pretty similar to this one that’s replaced it since, these charges being read aloud. A big one being going against the emperor, the charge of infant baptism, and then their view on the sacraments. So this is one of the charges from the clerk. Point number five says that they despised and scorned the mother of God and the saints. Michael Sattler’s answer to that was: “We do not dishonor the mother of God, for the mother of Christ is to be praised above all women, because God gave her the grace to give birth to the Savior of the whole world. And we do not revile the saints. But the Scriptures do not allow us to treat Mary or the saints as intercessors for us.” Point number six from the clerk: that he declared that one should not swear before a magistrate. He said simply, “The sixth charge is true, for swearing of oaths is forbidden by Christ himself.” Another of the charges, point number seven: that he has commenced a new and unheard of custom in regard to the Lord’s Supper, placing the bread and wine on a plate, eating and drinking of them. Can you give us more context on that charge? What did they think he was doing? Well, I’m assuming he’s following the procedure Conrad Grebel had given, which is: this is not transubstantiation. The bread and wine are not becoming the body and blood of Christ. So you don’t have this elaborate and special ceremony as in the Catholic Church. What he said was, serve it on a simple plate, and have someone without vestments, just one of the men in the group, share the bread and the wine. This sounds exactly like that. And so, just like the charge that you are dishonoring Mary: it seemed to them that if you won’t pray to Mary, you’re dishonoring her. And it seemed to them that if you just treat this wine and this bread as wine and bread, instead of as the consecrated body and blood of Christ, you’re dishonoring him. If you thought this really is the body and blood of Christ, that would be disrespectful. Another point here, again just quoting straight from the records we have. Point number eight: that contrary to the rule, he has married a wife. So give us some context on this. Well, read his reply. This response surprises me a little too. “As to my marriage, this is an ordinance of God.” Well, he did promise that he would be celibate. So you have to remember that. He is going against something he had promised earlier. The church did not always have celibate priests, but as the Middle Ages went on that became a requirement. So he’s going against what was expected. And I know they kind of winked at the fact that there were a lot of priests who had concubines. But he is saying, this is a good thing. So I think that’s the problem. 53:20 | The Turks The clerk, again, this is a quote: “He has said that if the Turks invaded the land, we ought not resist them. Does he approve of war?” This is a big one right here. His answer is very challenging. He says: “As regards the Turks, we will not fight them. For we are told in Scripture, thou shalt not kill. We are to beseech God with earnest prayers to repel and resist them. But if it were right for Christians to fight, I would rather go into battle against the so-called Christians who persecute, apprehend, and kill pious believers, than against the Turks. For the Turk is a genuine Turk and knows nothing of the Christian faith. But you claim to be Christians, boast of Christ, and still persecute the faithful witness of Christ. You are Turks according to the spirit.” Well, and you have to remember, the Turks had just crushed Hungary. They were threatening the empire. And if they captured Vienna, it would open the empire completely to their invasion. So this would sort of be like, when I was a young man, saying, I’m in favor of the Soviet Union and being taken over by them. Yes. And I can understand the feeling the non-Anabaptists had. But Sattler is saying that this is what God has called us to, to be non-resistant people in every situation. 54:57 | The Hangman Shall Dispute With You So it gets heated after that. Quote: “You wicked rogue, should we dispute with you? The hangman shall dispute with you.” And it feels like at this point the court, we don’t know for sure, devolves a bit from being a court proceeding to being: okay, we’re going to get you. We can’t believe you said that. You just crossed the line here. The hangman’s going to dispute with you. We know where this story is going to go. He makes this appeal now. He says, “Therefore, you ministers of God.” Now, I think that is a very interesting statement, how he’s referring to them. Just like the Schleitheim Confession: you ministers of God. He responds to that: “Therefore, you ministers of God, if you have not heard or read the Word of God, send for the most learned of your sacred books of the Bible and let them confer with us in the Word of God. If they prove to us by the Holy Scriptures that we err, we will gladly recant and suffer punishment. But if no error is found, I hope to God you will repent and receive instruction.” And then one of the replies to that statement is, quote, “It were better for you if you had never been born.” And he simply answers, “God knows what is good.” They continue to do a lot of mocking and threatening. Quote: “You arch-heretic, you have seduced the pious. If they would only now forsake their error.” And he simply answers, “Grace is with God alone.” And then one of the prisoners cries out, “We must not depart from the truth.” You can imagine the whole courtroom scene is getting a little heated. And you can see that in the response, because the next reply we have on record is, quote, “If there were no hangman here, I’d hang you myself, and I think I’d be doing God’s service.” At this point we don’t even need a conviction. We know where this is going to go. And the town clerk at this point turns to the judges and says, quote, “He will not stop today. Proceed with the sentence. I commit it to the law.” And finally, his reply to that was, “I am not sent to judge the Word of God in court. We are sent to bear witness of it. Therefore I cannot consent to any law unless shown otherwise by Scripture. I cannot be discharged. We are ready to suffer for the Word of God as long as breath remains in us.” And then again the clerk repeats what he has said before: “The hangman shall convince you, arch-heretic.” And he simply replies, “I appeal to the Scriptures.” And that’s it. 57:33 | Two Perspectives on Faithfulness We have two very different perspectives on what it means to be faithful. Again, it caused a kind of disruption even among the different non-Anabaptist people. Many of the key reformers, particularly those who knew him in Strasbourg, actually rose up and said, this is wrong. We were talking about how we’re in this place and it’s peaceful and all that. I really think the world is changing and has changed. And I think that doing what we’re doing is partly to waken us up. This could happen again. You are very right. And it might not look like it as we look at the people sitting around here with us. I think the things they’re committed to are shifting. And I think that as a people, we may become a rock of offense to them. So this is something important for us to think about. Amen. 58:36 | The Execution So we’re outside the city of Rottenburg now. Tell us about what happens next to Michael Sattler. The sentencing that comes down from the court: what happens to him at that point? Well, it was about a five minute drive to get out to this area, where it was known that they did these executions. And that path would have been gruesome. I’ll read a direct quote from the sentencing of what that would have been like, from the courthouse to here. Or from his prison house: it was a few days, and then he was taken here. It says, quote, “Michael Sattler shall be delivered to the executioner, who shall cut out his tongue, tear his body twice with red hot tongs on the wagon, and five more times beyond the city gate. Then he shall be burned to powder as a heretic.” And as a sign to his people who were here that this was bearable, he said he would raise two fingers. And when the cords holding him burned loose, he did do that. So the people were encouraged. He was staying faithful. And from here we know that Wilhelm Reublin, whose wife was one of those caught here, quickly published the account so people would know what was going on. And that caused a bit of a stir. But not only that: the public, and even the reformers he had a relationship with back in Strasbourg, when they heard about this, were very upset, and they wrote the authorities here complaining. And we have precious pieces of their letters that speak about their response. One is from Bucer. And Bucer was not known for just handing out compliments as a reformer there in Strasbourg. He said this in July of 1527: “We do not doubt that Michael Sattler, who was burned in Rottenburg, was a dear friend of God, although he was a leader of the Anabaptists, but much more skilled and honorable than some.” 60:35 | What Happened to Margaretha So what happened to Michael Sattler’s wife? She was part of this court trial as well. She had wanted to die with him, but they held her a few more days, and eventually they drowned her in the river nearby. And they tried to appeal to her, to get her to recant. There are some records that they actually worked on her for a while, but she stayed faithful. And there is some record that some of those women did recant. We hear that in the records. And she died by drowning, which they thought was the more merciful way to die, rather than burning at the stake. 61:09 | Next Episode: Pilgram Marpeck Accounts of Michael Sattler’s death on this very ground were quickly published, and they went viral. His witness was sealed not just in ink, but in fire, blood, and an unshakeable hope in God. And the movement did not die. Instead, it only grew more rapidly. In the next episode, we’ll encounter a mayor who was being pressured by the city council to persecute the Anabaptists. For months he wrestled with this, until one of those Anabaptists was burned at the stake and he could stand it no longer. He was overwhelmed by the testimony he witnessed. Within two weeks he had left everything and joined the Anabaptists. His name was Pilgram Marpeck, and he would quickly become one of the most significant Anabaptist leaders.
