title: Mayor to Radical Reformer
description: The Anabaptist Leader History Forgot: Mayor, Civil Engineer, Theologian
text: Episode 04      |    Pilgram Marpeck Mayor to Radical Reformer The Anabaptist Leader History Forgot: Mayor, Civil Engineer, Theologian 54 min 1495 – 1556 Rattenberg, Austria; Mikulov, Czechia; Strasbourg, France; Augsburg, Germany; About This Episode In the year 1528 in Rattenberg, Austria, a young man faced a crisis of conscience. He had it all: brilliant, wealthy, political connections, and mayor of the city at 30 years old. But then he was asked to persecute the Anabaptists. As the screams and the smoke drifted from the castle over his house, something changed in his heart, and he walked away from it all. In this episode, Dean Taylor, Stephen Russell, and Reagan Schrock follow Pilgram Marpeck through Europe and discuss his legacy, an important early Anabaptist leader that history nearly forgot. This documentary explores his significant contribution to the Anabaptist understanding of the sacraments, church life, and more. Anabaptist Origins is a 10-part documentary series produced by Anabaptist Perspectives that tells the story of the first hundred years of the Anabaptist movement. View Episode Credits Here: anabaptistorigins.org/credits/ Read the Transcript 0:00 | Cold Open: The Mayor Who Resigned One of the most fascinating leaders of the Anabaptists is a man history almost forgot. His name was Pilgram Marpeck, and he was born and lived right here in Rattenberg. His house is just down the hill from this castle. Talented, successful, and brilliant, he was appointed to the city council by age 18. By age 30, he was mayor. Throughout that time, Anabaptists were coming through this region, and the city cracked down hard on these new teachings. On January 1, 1528, Pilgram Marpeck requested not to have to prosecute the Anabaptists. On January 3, he was ordered to comply. On January 10, he attempted to fulfill those orders. On January 14, an Anabaptist was executed right here at this castle. Two weeks later, Pilgram Marpeck resigned. 1:26 | Rattenberg and the Tyrol We’re at a pretty significant place, a very narrow little alpine city where Pilgram Marpeck was born, right here. And he lived in this house. This is the home he would have left from. Why don’t you give us some more context on this region as a whole, so we can figure out what the context was that Marpeck was coming from? This region here is called the Tyrol, and it was under the Habsburgs. This was really an important area for them because it was a major mining area. They got a lot of their wealth from the silver and other minerals that were mined here. It was a really important piece of Habsburg territory. One of the things that’s really interesting for us is that this was one of the hotspots for Anabaptist conversion. Right at the very beginning, Blaurock came here. He left Switzerland, came here, and this just proved to be a really fruitful field. And then after that, many, many people came. If you go from when Blaurock was here to close to the end of the 1500s, we think there were 20,000 converts from this area. Most of them were either killed, because the Habsburgs were rabidly anti-Anabaptist, or they mostly went to Moravia. There they established Hutterite colonies. Some of them were more Swiss Brethren. This was a really important place for us. Looking into some of the details of that mining area gives you an idea. You’ve got a bunch of radicals who aren’t able to fit into society very well. You can find work here. They employed, in one record I read, over 50,000 miners who came from Austria, Italy, around Europe, to find work here. They had 68 miles of tunnels from the miners here. That’s an incredible amount. This particular place and another place called Schwaz were the two main mining areas. So I think you could probably double the mining miles if you looked at that area. And then another thing that happened around here with all those thousands of men: we have records of a lot of reformers, still Catholic, some Lutherans, some just radicals, who would come here and preach in these areas. There are records of them meeting in the thousands, hearing about these new ideas of salvation by faith, or criticism about the things that were happening and the way we need to change things. And in that, they’re smuggling Bibles, they’re smuggling pamphlets, and people are starting to talk. That’s the kind of atmosphere Pilgram would have been raised in. 4:11 | A Rising Man So, a little bit about his particular life. Pilgram was born here, and this was where he moved from. His father would have been very successful. Heinrich became very wealthy in the work here, and actually became mayor himself. But when it comes to Pilgram: at 18 years old he was already on the city council. By age 25 he started his own business transporting ore. It was so successful that he’s on record at the highest tax bracket here. There are records of him actually loaning money to Archduke Ferdinand himself, at 5 percent interest. 4:45 | The Habsburg Brothers One of the very important dynasties, and maybe the most important dynasty we’re going to hear about all throughout the documentary, is the Habsburgs. At the beginning there were Habsburgs in Spain, and that’s Charles the Emperor, Charles V. And there were Habsburgs here in Austria, and that’s the Archduke Ferdinand. They’re brothers, and they’re both strongly Catholic, strongly anti-Anabaptist. And as long as the Emperor is alive, Charles V pretty much controls this whole area. When he retires, I said dies, but he’s an emperor who retired from his job rather than died and left it behind. I believe the year was 1558. His son got the western part of the Habsburg lands. That would be the Netherlands. That would be a part of France close to the Rhine River. It would have been Spain, and it would have included southern Italy. Then Ferdinand would have gotten the lands in Germany and Austria. He was then chosen emperor. 5:59 | Mayor at Thirty So by age 30 he’s made mayor, and then at 31, Archduke Ferdinand himself personally appointed him as the leader of the mining districts of this region. That would have been a high level job. Because when we walked up here, we’re looking at this and it’s a nice house. You’re looking down the street thinking, that’s a nice house. That’s the same thing we said when we were in Zurich, sitting in front of what used to be Conrad Grebel’s house. Look at it. This is nice. His dad was an aristocrat. His dad was on the city council. There was money in that family. Same thing with Marpeck. What a unique character. Not really the profile I would have thought of as a significant Anabaptist leader. 6:41 | An Engineer Who Knew Latin His education was different from Conrad’s and the others, but he was still brilliant. Tell us a little about how he would have been educated. Well, I don’t believe he went to university, but he would have known Latin. The thing that really stands out is that he learned engineering. That’s what made him useful. That’s why he could direct the mining here. And the mining wasn’t just digging into the ground. It included chopping trees down higher up, and then sluicing them down where they could be used further below. I would say the two key things were that he was well read, but he knew Latin and he knew engineering. And knowing Latin meant that he also read extensively. When he decides to leave the Catholics, he first becomes Lutheran. But he doesn’t like everything. And then eventually he becomes an Anabaptist. And right out of the starting gate he’s engaging in deep theological concerns. You can see that his upbringing produced a true Renaissance man type of person. He had the engineering, he had the theology, he had the understanding right from the start. And also well read in the early church writings. It’s interesting, particularly when he gets to the balance, and we’ll talk about that a little bit, talking about his views of the sacraments. He’s arguing against two sides. And in those, you’re hearing him quote Tertullian, quoting the early Christians. And even here in this mining town, he was well read in the patristics. 8:16 | The Miners The Tyrol was a main source of Habsburg wealth because of the silver, the lead, the salt, all kinds of minerals they could extract. This city and another one called Schwaz were two of the main industrial centers making that wealth. The miners were not always treated really well. You mentioned they came from all over. And you don’t have to treat a foreigner so well. So that’s probably part of it. But anyway, those who were not treated well already knew the Christian message by and large. But now they’re hearing that Jesus makes us all God’s sons and daughters, that we’re all in the image of God. And it’s not that the people who heard this message and accepted it wanted to throw off all authority. But they saw a real distinction between how you, the lord, live, and how I, the miner, live. So that was a big part of what drew them. 9:22 | The Castle Above the Town This was an important Habsburg center, and this castle would have been their seat of authority in this area. You’ve got up on these cliffs the castle, which is fairly large, and then the city down below. Now, I don’t know this for sure, but I imagine that a trial would have been held there, because this is probably where the Habsburg official stayed. He had his position. He was wealthy. He had a reputation. A beautiful place to live. He had his wife, children. To give that up for something inside of him, something that drove him, a faith that he didn’t see in his life. And he traded all that prosperity to follow Jesus. Think about a modern day contrast. A very wealthy businessman. He’s got a family, a nice house. You’re so rich you’re loaning money out to the president. And yet someone like that looks at their life and says, actually, no, I don’t really have it all. I’m missing something. That’s a significant part of the story for really all of these early Anabaptists. They had pretty good lives. Michael Sattler, you’re the prior of the monastery. Pretty good life. He was well off. But he looks at that and says, no, something’s missing here. And I need to dig into what that is. I’ll give up the whole world to follow Jesus. 10:49 | Ordered to Prosecute So by 1527, known Anabaptists started to be persecuted here. And here’s the thing. They asked Pilgram Marpeck to be part of the persecuting of these Anabaptists. And he complied as best he could. He tried to find a middle ground. He would actually go through a lot of trouble to go to the courts and try to get lighter sentences for them, to change things for them. And then it was actually given as part of his job description that it was for him to do this. And then we have on record that he formally requested in 1528 not to be a part of this. I don’t want to do this anymore. This isn’t part of the job. This isn’t what I signed up for. And that began to eat at him. But then a very gifted Anabaptist, whom we’re even going to talk about a little bit in our episode about the Hutterite mission machine, is Leonhard Schiemer. Schiemer is the one who wrote the famous thing about the flask. Some people say we convert people so much that you must be drinking some kind of potion. There’s some kind of magic involved. And he gives them an answer. We’ll give that answer later. But this is where he dies. He’s captured here, and the laws were that he was going to be prosecuted and persecuted and put to the end of his life. 12:08 | Fourteen Days in January So again: on January 1st we have on record that he formally requested, I don’t want to be a part of this. January 3rd, we have on record that he was ordered to comply. January 10th, we have orders showing that he was actually trying to do that. So we do see him just wrestling. You can literally get into where he’s wrestling with this. On January 14th, Leonhard Schiemer was condemned to die by burning. Probably by Marpeck’s working, they said, no, we’ll just execute him by cutting his head off. And so they released a sentence that he not be burned at the stake. And then Marpeck has to experience that whole thing of him dying there. And then something happened. The records seem to indicate that he was executed here. At the castle? Right. This is the Habsburg castle. He was tried here, executed here. They had to cut off his head, and then maybe down there or up here somewhere they would have burned him. 13:02 | Close Enough to Smell the Smoke We can obviously see through the record that he was wrestling with this. And then consider that he could even perhaps have smelled the smoke. Look how close this is to where the execution happened. And again, for context, this is Habsburg Empire, Catholic. They’re very much of the mind, we don’t want the Anabaptists here. Marpeck is in the local politics of this city, city council, mayor and so forth. And we clearly have records of him struggling through this, trying to find the middle road, trying to play in both worlds. And you have this Anabaptist who’s executed right here at this castle. We’re at the overlook here where the castle wall is built onto this. And Marpeck’s house is right down here, where he was born and raised, all the way up until this incident. You can imagine when they burn this Anabaptist after they behead him, the smoke would have traveled right here. You can imagine Marpeck thinking, wow. You would have heard the commotion. You would have smelled the smell. And we know this: two weeks later he resigns and leaves town and becomes an Anabaptist. Sometime also during this period, and we don’t know the exact time, his wife dies. And from here, Pilgram Marpeck becomes one of the main leaders of the Anabaptists. 14:33 | Moravia Marpeck leaves Rattenberg very soon after this execution and comes here, to Moravia, which is now the modern day Czech Republic. And during this time period he married Anna and moved here. This Moravian area becomes very important, not just for understanding Pilgram Marpeck, but for understanding the early Anabaptists in general, because it allows a spot where he discusses things that are more conservatively leaning one way or more liberal leaning the other, more Spiritualist in one way, more Catholic in the other. And so a lot comes out in Moravia. So yes, he comes here, probably coming into the different communitarian and non-communitarian radicals of the Radical Reformation who are here. And he tends to be with them for a while. It seems this is the place where he was baptized, he and Anna. So he begins to grow and develop his Anabaptist conviction. And he’s quickly an organizer. I think that shows off his skills from the workplace. So he gets baptized, he gets ordained or put into some sort of leadership. We don’t have any of those details, and most historians say he probably ends up in the Austerlitz area. Pilgram Marpeck is a favorite, particularly for the historian types who dig into it. He’s a favorite for many reasons, because we see him as sort of this middle ground guy. And I know as historians it’s considered wrong to put our image onto historic figures. It’s an anachronism to do that. On the other hand, it’s also wrong to think of these people as totally different from us. And when I read Marpeck, and I read about these circles that were here in this Moravian area, it seems like I really can relate. 16:35 | Between the Hutterites and the Spiritualists For instance, this becomes, later on after he goes to Strasbourg, and we’re going to go there next, a connection he always keeps. And in that connection you’re seeing him have conflicts early on with the Hutterites. He loved the zeal and the mission drive and everything. But there was what he considered to be a forced community of goods. In other words, to join the community it was a rule, you had to have complete community of goods. He loved community of goods, but forced, no, that’s too much. Later on he’s writing to Spiritualists. When he gets to Strasbourg, we’ll talk about that, and you see his writings. But then even later in his life you see him writing to people who have taken his ideas and said, okay, we don’t need any of those kinds of regulations. And he’s telling them, no, come back. And so it’s a fascinating piece. It allows us to dig into the different personalities of the different Anabaptist communities right from the beginning. From here, let’s go to Strasbourg, where he really settles in and you start to see him trying to work with Reformers, trying to still write letters to different places. I think we’ll really see him shining as one of the very interesting figures in early Anabaptism. 17:51 | Strasbourg: An Open City As we discussed in the Michael Sattler episode, Strasbourg is a place where there’s a lot of transition. It’s one of the last places to actually establish a state church. Capito and Bucer don’t go there right away. And that opens the door for lots of other people to come here. I think the two men were more inclined to try to convince people rather than to persecute them. So it was an open city. September 1528 was the date. Now, when he got here, this was already a bit of a hub of Anabaptists. There were approximately 250 Anabaptists already in the city. And Michael Sattler had come through here. And in particular, not too long before he got here, there was a big debate with Hans Denck. That stirred up some differences between the Anabaptists and the Reformers. From that point the Reformers didn’t attack the Anabaptists, but they wouldn’t do public disputations with them anymore. They did have private ones, like with Sattler. Something about the Denck disputation didn’t go well in their opinion. But I don’t know what it was. So it’s interesting that here in Strasbourg a lot of the early leaders came through, and they almost just seemed to miss each other. Michael Sattler, as we covered in the last episode, came in 1527. Here in 1528 we have Pilgram Marpeck. In 1529 we have Melchior Hoffman coming here, and we’ll be talking about him a little bit later. They overlap. And Marpeck is not happy with what Hoffman has to say. That’s one part of the story I just didn’t know before doing this trip: how many Anabaptists flowed through here. It was a bit of a safe haven that allowed them to get some things down on paper, to solidify some things. And it makes sense that Pilgram Marpeck ends up in the same spot. 20:06 | Schwenckfeld and Hans Denck So it’s not just that the Anabaptist groups are here, but there were also different radicals on the fringes of Anabaptism, like Schwenckfeld. Tell us a little about that, the Spiritualists who were here in this area. Schwenckfeld felt that the church was so corrupt that it was really impossible to start a new church until a new word from God came. So they stopped baptism. They stopped the Lord’s Supper. It’s not that they didn’t think these were right and things they should do. They just thought they needed another word from God. The Anabaptists said, no, we’ve already got that Word. It’s the New Testament. However, there were a lot of things about the Anabaptists, the fact that they pointed to the interior so much, not exclusively, that drew the Spiritualists to them. Marpeck’s biggest fight was with Schwenckfeld. And this is the first time Marpeck meets Schwenckfeld and starts getting to that, because his later writings pull out a lot of his incarnational teachings, where he is having to balance between these Spiritualists here. Now, wouldn’t Hans Denck also have been in that camp? Well, Hans Denck is a really interesting person who seems to have one foot pretty much with the evangelical Anabaptists, our ancestors, and one with the Spiritualists. At the end of his life he dies from the plague. At the end of his life he writes something called the Recantation, but it seems he is simply saying, what we did was too much. We should have been slower and not as hard-pushing as we were. It doesn’t seem like he’s really saying, I wish I hadn’t been baptized, but rather that the whole thing was probably inappropriate considering where the society was. 22:03 | The Waterworks So that’s some context for where Pilgram Marpeck is coming to at the time. But you mentioned this earlier, Dean: what were maybe some other reasons they might have ended up in this city? It must have been attractive. Remember his role there in the mines, with his parents and everything, and what he was raised in. So when he came here in September of 1528, he got a job working in the waterworks. One of the charms of Strasbourg is still these canals they built to move timber. And he particularly, in this spot, was moving those logs through here, and that gave him employment. I wish we could find specifics. We know he built that piece right there. We looked. We tried. We searched and searched. But what you’re describing is someone who’s pretty important to the functioning of the city. The waterworks, the hydraulic systems, bringing timber in from the Black Forest into the city for its many uses. Did he have a job offer, or do we even know? It’s not written in the records the way it is later when we get to Augsburg, but we do know that he had this position, and that he became a citizen in 1531. It’s a part of Marpeck that’s so fascinating, and why he becomes a favorite of a lot of people, because he tried to engage with the community. He was a real citizen while still being a true citizen of the kingdom of God. I think that’s an impressive part of him. Still pastoring, but working with people every day in places like this. That would have been really fascinating. 23:36 | Expelled There is something else that should be said. Whereas Sattler seems to have had a very peaceful time with the Reformers here, Marpeck must have been a little bit more driving, because they actually expelled him. It’s a good point. I like a lot of what he says. I just think it’s interesting that there is a contrast here. So he had a lot going for him. All that he’d been through in his journey: he lost a wife, got married again, went to Moravia, started meeting the Anabaptists there, took some kind of leadership in Moravia, was sent here, and got into leadership pretty soon here. And from here he seems to have been writing letters all the way from the Tyrol Anabaptists to the northern areas here. He had a pretty big footprint as an early Anabaptist leader, and he had a good job. Then things went wrong. December 18th, 1531, the government said, okay, we like what you’re doing, but you’re going to need to bear arms in case we get attacked, and you’re going to have to give an oath of allegiance to the government. And again you see the conviction and the integrity. He had this great position. I can’t do it. He did ask for a little bit more time, and they did give that to him. So that’s to the credit of the council. But ultimately he has to leave the city. It’s a remarkable chapter and a remarkable leader. 25:04 | The Missing Twelve Years And from here there are 12 years. We don’t know exactly where he was. He did go to Switzerland, we know that. And then maybe he came back here every now and then. There seem to be some records. Probably not in the city, but he had congregations in the countryside. Pilgram Marpeck had to leave Strasbourg. Where does he go after that? Well, there are 12 years in which we don’t know the details. We do know he was in Moravia, and we know he was in eastern Switzerland. And we do know that in eastern Switzerland he used his engineering skills to build a linen production factory. That was between St. Gallen and Appenzell. But other than that we don’t have much detail. 25:50 | Augsburg: Master of the Waterworks What we do know is that in 1544 he accepted a job right here in Augsburg, in current Augsburg, Germany, as the master of the waterworks of this place. These waterworks, as we can see even here in Augsburg, are still charming today. It’s a World Heritage Site. In 2019 the whole waterworks system here became a protected World Heritage Site. And that would have been a very high position. Of course, as we were talking about in Strasbourg, he would have had all that experience there and was able to bring it here. It even has in the court records how much money he received. It says he took 150 guilders a year. Looking that up in current money, it’s not an exorbitant amount, but it’s well middle class, upper middle class. And he would have also had, it seems, a nice place to live for him and Anna. Looking at this stunning 16th century map, we can almost trace the path of the log. These canals would have been used for several things. They were able to bring clean water in and bad water out. It was able to help with sewage. It helped them bring transportation into the city. But particularly with Pilgram Marpeck, it was able to bring large logs from the forestry into here that people could use for craftsmen and this type of thing. It was an extraordinary process that they had here. Pilgram Marpeck helped with the cutting, the transporting, and the distribution of the wood, and its building projects, and it supported all the different industries. Now, the house where he lived, we don’t know exactly, but we have some precious little clues. We can find St. Moritz Church. There’s some discrepancy on this. We know that he was close to the waterworks. Some of the books say it’s north. It might have been what people were referring to as north in the way the map is structured. But closer up toward where the waterworks were is where it’s thought that Pilgram Marpeck and Anna lived. Now, also a little interesting side note with Anna: there are some records that make it sound like she possibly was a midwife, working with the different refugee populations here, which is also a fascinating detail of the Marpecks in this city. 28:17 | A Bivocational Pastor Under Reprimand So here it’s a little more quiet. We don’t have a lot of personal letters. We do have some works he’s done. But this piece, with his years of experience from his childhood to Strasbourg to here, is that we really see an Anabaptist leader who is a bivocational worker, putting his skills to work but still pastoring in all his free time. And it seems his wife rode alongside him. Very inspiring leader. One thing about here: the city government knew that he was pastoring an Anabaptist congregation. And they scolded him for that. There are several places in the official writings where it gives his salary and says that they reprimanded him and wanted him to stop. But he must have been pretty useful and helpful, because they never followed through on that. Where he starts, he was under the Habsburgs, and they weren’t going to tolerate him despite his abilities. In Strasbourg he was pretty aggressive, more so than Sattler, and so the Protestant church leaders there got to not like him and expelled him. And that’s how he ends up here. We don’t know much about what happened in St. Gallen and Appenzell when he built that linen processing plant. Then he came here. But everywhere, he obviously was a man of skill, and where he caused too much friction, perhaps, he needed to leave. Or where the Catholics were Habsburgs and were not going to allow him to stay. There was only a small Anabaptist congregation here, a very small one. So historians question, why did you move there? It does seem to be connected with this position, and he was still able to minister to this area in that way. And you’re right, writing a statement of faith got him in trouble, and it is in the record that they rebuked him for it. But they just let it go. 30:21 | Back at Rattenberg: What He Cared About We’re right here in Rattenberg. I can literally see that Marpeck’s house is right there, and where the Anabaptist executions happened, 71 according to the plaque up there, 71 executions up at the castle. I can see that from here, and how that so deeply affected Pilgram Marpeck. Let’s get a little deeper. What were the things he wrote about, talked about, cared about? I think it would be good to talk about some of the things that were either unique to him, or at least were his strengths. There are at least two things I would like us to talk about. One of them is his view of how to do discipline. All the Anabaptists believed you should have a discipled church, but sometimes there needed to be discipline. So he has an interesting take on that. We’re going to talk a little bit about his view of the sacraments, but that is actually part of a broader thing. He had a very incarnational understanding of how God worked in the world. He believed that both the physical and the spiritual were important. 31:28 | The Spiritualist Pull That was a big problem area for the Anabaptists. Your emphasis on the internal, that we actually turn to Jesus, makes us liable to go toward the Spiritualist side. One of the big groups, and I don’t mean in size but in influence at the beginning of the Reformation, was the Spiritualists. That was often a tension point. One of the early Anabaptists was Hans Denck. Seeking to know God as deeply as possible spiritually isn’t bad. But he may have gone a little bit too far the other way. In fact, Hans Denck said that as long as I have the Word, meaning Jesus, inside of me, I don’t need the Word, the written Word. So he took it pretty far. That’s how far the Spiritualists came. And like I said, the real body of Spiritualists said, we just can’t do any of this. We’ve got to wait. And so that did pull on us. One of the really good things about Marpeck is that he recognized that what it means to be a human is to be a physical body and a soul, a spirit. As we look through history, so many times it’s those opponents that help give us the documents we have. And in arguing with Schwenckfeld and these hyper-spiritualists, we get this beautiful incarnational theology. 33:00 | Marpeck on the Sacraments One of my favorite parts about Marpeck is his view of the sacraments. Now, when you’re reading any of the Anabaptist discussions about sacraments, you have to keep the context in mind. What all of them, all the Reformation, many within the Catholic Church and the Reformation churches were arguing against, was the idea they call ex opere operato, the idea that from the act it happens, no matter what, mechanically. And so many people within both the Catholic Church and the Reformed Church were saying, there’s got to be faith. There’s got to be something inside that’s reality. So you see people like Hubmaier and Marpeck and several others make the argument, pushing back on the way they’re doing these mechanical sacraments. And they’re saying, did you forget to read 1 Corinthians 11, where it says that what you’re doing is not the Lord’s Supper? So somewhere along the way, morality matters. Real life matters. And they’re not saying that if you have any sin you can’t have a sacrament, or that somebody has to be perfect. A lot of people like to say, oh, this is a Donatist thing all over again, and you have to be perfect. They’re not saying that. But they are saying it’s got to be real, and there’s got to be faith. And so in developing this, you get a rich tradition, if you understand what the context is. One of my favorite quotes from Marpeck comes out of his discussions with Schwenckfeld. And he says this, and I think it puts it in an excellent way. He says: He’s saying, like the Marburg Colloquy and all these debates about the metaphysics and everything: guys, you need to put this aside and look inside. You’re missing the most important part. And then he goes on: That’s pretty strong. 36:05 | Faith With an Outward Working So I think that balance we see in there, the genuineness. Where we’re getting into all these debates, and he’s asking, has your life changed? And talking about that: maybe if we would read not just Marpeck, but if we would read the early Anabaptists, they did not say, okay, just give your life to the Lord and that’s it. You read in there that we have to struggle on the inside. That was a consistent theme throughout Anabaptism. Not, okay, turn your life over to the Lord and everything will be grand. They would say things like, Christ has to be born in you and grow in you, and it’s going to hurt. In other words, they took a very realistic understanding. Like you were saying, Marpeck would say: internally, you have to have faith and you have to believe this, but it also has to have an outward working. So the Father is the spiritual, and the Son, who came as man, is the physical. The two main things they looked at were baptism and the Lord’s Supper. It has to have that internal spiritual part, and it has to have the physical part. Zwingli would have said, this is just a sign. The communion is just a sign. He also would say, to bring in another sacrament, that he accused us of being legalists because we care when the baptism happens. You are either chosen by God or not. You’re either elect or not. So it doesn’t matter if you’re baptized before you know that or after. And we say, no, there’s actually free will involved here. You have to hear the gospel, respond to it, and then ask to be baptized. There’s a reason for the order. 38:09 | Let Them Be Born First On that same thought, I remember one of the arguments. Zwingli and Luther, and Calvin too, would really push the point hard on eighth-day circumcision and say: look at the babies in the Old Covenant. They’re born, and then on the eighth day we would circumcise them. So why can’t you see it as the same thing in the New Testament? And we baptize babies on the eighth day. The Anabaptists answered, we agree with you, but you must let them be born first. Born again. And that’s the point. So being born by faith into the kingdom of God. That makes sense. It ties up the whole thing. But that is so counter to what had been taught for so long. However you said it, by the act itself. You just go through the mechanics of it and boom, the thing happens. Catholics recognized that when someone chose to join a monastery, something is happening. And sometimes they called that their second baptism. That is important. In other words, they even saw instinctively, I think, that baptism is a marker for when I’ve turned around somehow. So if I live in Rattenberg and then I decide, I really want to serve the Lord, I’m going to join the monastery, they don’t baptize you again. Those vows they sometimes saw as your second baptism. 39:44 | Church Life and Discipline So we just went through a bit of Marpeck’s sacramental theology. I’m curious, how is he looking at the life of the church? What is church life like? Dig into that a bit. I know he did some writing on that. It’s interesting. During the early Anabaptist period they had a lot of things in common. By far, particularly the ones that survived, had a lot in common. All of them believed in community of some kind. All of them believed in discipline and order. But how you worked out your community, what the lines of your community were, differed from community to community. And Marpeck represents a circle that tried not to be so spelled out. In my opinion, for what it’s worth, I see Marpeck as a very charismatic, very successful, formerly wealthy, very capable man who just had natural leadership. And so I think around him you just grew a community. He does say some very good things about when the church needs to discipline. I think we can learn from him, but I also think we can learn from the others. 40:58 | The Bud and the Fruit I agree. We should not put him in this libertine window. No, he’s not libertine. Exactly. Because he’s criticizing maybe the Hutterites and the Swiss Brethren, he’s not saying just live freely. That’s not what he’s saying. Well, yes, but his group died out. Now, what he said that’s really good, as far as going overboard, is that what we should do is not look at a bud on a tree. We shouldn’t look at the little leaves starting to come out. We need to see what the fruit is. That’s when you judge. Now, if you see a bud that makes you suspicious, that’s the time to talk. He is exactly right. But I don’t know if he actually passed it on. His criticism is really good, but it kind of dies with Marpeck. It seems to. But maybe we’ve rediscovered it since 1950 to help us think this through. His incarnational material is wonderful. His moderation about how to approach discipline is wonderful. But we all fail. 42:16 | Structure and Belonging So I’m only saying that perhaps we’ve got a good pattern here. When I first became Beachy, I was 20. And I came because of nonresistance. And they said, dress this way. Well, they never really clearly explained why. But who cares? I wanted what’s good here. And I saw many good things. I saw community. I saw nonresistance. And so I really wanted to belong. But how I dressed didn’t matter so much to me. Well, then when I was in my 30s, I had several experiences where I saw that everybody cares how they dress. Everybody cares how they dress. And everybody follows somebody. When I saw that, it just flipped everything. Okay, I know why we do this now. The others, I think, had a little more structure. So you’re saying the others, as in at the time of Marpeck. The other Anabaptists would have had more structure. They would have read Schleitheim. They would have seen how their other congregations were forming. And this does seem a bit more charismatically led. And so both things together are really good. And so I love this guy. I’m not putting him down. I’m saying, though, that some of his critique, perhaps, of the Swiss Brethren was a bit strong. Let me read you one real quick, straight from the book: So it’s pretty strong stuff. It goes through several things saying that. 44:10 | Wrestling With New Questions Well, as a person who studies church history and loves it, the Scriptures give us the foundation. But there are always new questions coming up. And somebody has to wrestle with those and say, this is what is meant. And that almost misses that. Now, I am absolutely sure Marpeck was a Trinitarian Christian. I’m absolutely sure. He would have said he believes the Apostles’ Creed. But that came from somewhere. It came from wrestling. I’ll give you an example. In the early church, they read in the Scriptures: God the Father, God the Son, God the Spirit, and yet there’s one God. What does that mean? They wrestled for hundreds of years, and they came up with either the Apostles’ Creed or the Nicene Creed, whichever one you want to think about. Also, there were Scriptures that said Jesus is man and Jesus is God. What does that mean? So they wrestled with these things, and they came out with good explanations, as far as we can understand in this present life. But my point is that the church has wrestled all the way through time with new questions, and they had to look to the Scriptures. We can both look back at how the church wrestled with these kinds of ideas, and also recognize that some things have been dealt with. For instance, Jesus is the picture of what it means to be a human. So we’ve got to go back to that, wrestle with it the way they did. But it’s not just something you pull out of the Bible. I’m an Anabaptist. I’ve chosen to be an Anabaptist. Sometimes I think they misunderstood where they were coming from. They actually got some good things from their Catholic tradition. And so finding their way through those balances, I think, is what some of these early days were doing. I wonder what would have happened if, instead of being persecuted, they were maybe shunted aside, but with a “we’ll let you be Anabaptist,” and they could have gotten together and talked these things over. They already did some wonderful, amazing things, like the Schleitheim conference. I don’t know how they got in touch with the right people and got them there, but they did conferences secretly, often. 46:32 | Nachfolge Christi Like other Anabaptists, his approach was Nachfolge Christi, the discipleship of Christ. We follow Christ. He taught a cross that was not just substitutionary, it was participatory. And if you want to look into early church history, look up Christus Victor. It’s that what saves us is our participation in the humanity of Christ. Christ did everything we should have done instead of the fall. Living that out. And so he lived out the perfect human life. We are participating with him, and we’re drawing our life from him, and gradually, painfully but gradually, we’re becoming more and more like him. By the grace of God. 47:20 | A Leader Willing to Take Risks So Pilgram Marpeck was quite the guy. He really was. He was a leader who was willing to take risks, both personally and theologically. We think of his hometown, the place where he was raised, where he had everything a man could want. And when he came to radical Christianity, truly following Christ, he was able to give it all up. When he went to Strasbourg and finally made it there again, doing well, leading a church, but when pressed, again he said, I’ll leave. Even theologically, when he had some of his people he was close to seeming to deny parts of the incarnation, or become Spiritualist, he really brought in a rich, deep, historic Christianity, defending many of his views, both his sacramental views and his theological views, with a rich historical incarnational theology that comes out in a lot of his teachings. He was quite a person. 48:21 | What Happened to Marpeck, and the Kunstbuch My question then is, what happened to Pilgram Marpeck? Well, he lived here and worked for the government until 1556, and then the record of paying him ends. He died here peacefully. He wasn’t martyred. One of the interesting things about him, though, is that we did have some of his writings already in the early 1900s, but in the 1950s Delbert Gratz discovered a significant-sized book called the Kunstbuch, which means the art book. It has a lot of Marpeck’s writings, but it also has the writings of his circle. It’s written very artistically, and that gave us a lot more information about him. At this point we have records, official documents, something like we might have for Menno. Some of the significant things about him are his recognition of the importance of the incarnation, that God became one of us. But one that I think is also significant is his understanding of how to use the ban. All the Anabaptists believed in using the ban, but he felt that some were too ready to use it. And maybe because he had actually lived in eastern Switzerland for a while, and he felt the Swiss were too strict, that might be one reason he wrote about this. 49:46 | Next Episode: The Martyrs’ Synod In this same city of Augsburg, Anabaptist leaders would meet in secret to plan a strategy for missions. History would remember this as the Martyrs’ Synod, because nearly every man who attended would soon die. These evangelists, joined by the newly organized Hutterites, would carry the message of Christ further than ever before. In the next episode, we’ll come face to face with true missional dedication, and the men and women who gave up everything to carry the message of Jesus across a broken continent. Previous Episode Seven Intolerable Truths – Episode 03 Next Episode “They Grow Only to Be Cut Down” – Episode 05

title: “They Grow Only to Be Cut Down”
description: Hutterites: the Radical Missionaries of the Radical Reformation
text: Episode 05      |    Balthasar Hubmaier, Jacob Hutter, Peter Riedemann “They Grow Only to Be Cut Down” Hutterites: the Radical Missionaries of the Radical Reformation 55 min 1525 – 1556 Augsburg, Germany; Mikulov, Czechia; Falkenstein, Austria; Gmunden, Austria: Innsbruck, Austria; Vienna, Austria About This Episode A passion was brewing in the streets of Augsburg in 1527, a burning desire in the early Anabaptists to spread the faith. This drive was so relentless that nearly all who attended the infamous “Martyrs Synod” would be martyred for their missionary zeal. Dean Taylor, Stephen Russell, and Reagan Schrock guide you through the incredible church growth that resulted from this early Anabaptist missionary zeal. This documentary introduces the key groups and individuals who played a role in that growth. Perhaps the most inspiring story is that of the Hutterites and their early leaders such as Jacob Hutter and Peter Riedemann. These leaders refused to take up the sword, in contrast to another Anabaptist leader: Balthasar Hubmaier. Persecuted and exiled, these first Hutterites’ perseverance in laying down their lives to spread the Gospel is a resounding challenge to the church today. Anabaptist Origins is a 10-part documentary series produced by Anabaptist Perspectives that tells the story of the first hundred years of the Anabaptist movement. View Credits Here: anabaptistorigins.org/credits/ Read the Transcript 0:00 | Cold Open: The Martyrs’ Synod In August 1527, the city of Augsburg is divided between Catholic and Protestant and crawling with informants. Somewhere here, a group of men met in secret in an ordinary house. They came not with weapons or banners, but with one word burning in their bones: Go. In a time when kingdoms were falling, these men met not to seize power for themselves, but to build the church. They had walked through fire to be here. History would remember this as the Martyrs’ Synod. Within just a few short years, nearly all of them would be dead. 1:14 | Looking for the House So Dean, we’re here in Augsburg, Germany, and I want to find this place where the Martyrs’ Synod actually happened. Do we know where that is? Where can we look for this? Unfortunately, we don’t know exactly. But we do have some pretty good clues, somewhere in these windy roads of Augsburg. And I love that we still have these old roads. We know that this happened in an ordinary house. Now, this one gives us something that’s at least a hint. This was a plaque put up for a raid that happened on an Anabaptist house a year later. We know the Synod was somewhere around here, and there’s a good chance it was in this area. Here, 80 Anabaptists were arrested, many of them martyred. So it gives us an idea: just a common house. Nothing fancy. So this was 80 in here. They had 60 at the Synod. So it would be something like this where they were all coming. 2:07 | The World in 1527 Literally at this moment, the Pope in Rome was overrun. Charles V’s mutinous troops had taken over, and he’s actually hiding. He goes from the Vatican over to the Castel Sant’Angelo, where he was hiding during this time. The Muslims, we know, had already taken a jihad coming up over Hungary, and were now advancing, wanting to put flags in the Habsburg areas. We know that with all these things happening, there was a lot of persecution and fear. You could imagine the emperors, and everybody was upset. But they came trying to find a practical way to put into practice the teachings of Jesus about the littlest of the commands that he has in the Bible, and that is the command: Go. Go and preach the gospel. And so that’s why they gathered. It was an interesting group. When you look at the list of the people who were there, and we do have a list of who was there, we have a remarkable amount of information about this and what they did here. Their passion to spread the kingdom of God was just really amazing to me. It gives me the sense that this is a special place. 3:22 | What Had Happened Since Zurich We’re in 1527. A lot has happened. We just had the first baptisms in January of 1525, and this is only two years later. So much has been happening since. Give us a bit of a rundown of what’s been going on since those first baptisms. It’s a good idea, because it is remarkable, and wow, there’s a lot that’s happened. So let’s take it back a little. We were there in Zurich. 1525 was the first baptism. Right after that illegal act they hit the mission field, and we talked about that, and how they went to far different places. In 1526, Lord Liechtenstein had opened up Moravia. That’s the Czech Republic now, way east of where they are. We already see people start heading there. By January of 1527 we see Felix Manz, after preaching and coming back and escaping and coming back, martyred there in the Limmat River. And we were there. By the next month, February 24th, Michael Sattler up in Schleitheim is putting together the Schleitheim Confession. By May of that same year, 1527, he’s burned at the stake. But then in August of 1527, somehow that word got out across Europe to all of these radical people, and they met here to discuss what they were going to do. 4:40 | A War Room, Not a Retreat The thing that strikes me is, this isn’t like a little pastors’ conference, or, hey, how do we survive extreme persecution? Though I’m sure there was some of that. The motive, and what they’re discussing, is pretty different from that. It really is. It wasn’t a retreat. This was no pastors’ retreat. This was a war room. However, they were not in any way wanting to use the weapons of this world, but to walk under the weapons of Christ. And they preached a very radical message. When they came together, they formed a plan to send out two by two, sometimes three, into the different parts of Europe to spread this message. 5:27 | Laying Down Views to Work Together Another thing impressive about it is the groups of people they brought together. It’s amazing to hear that these radicals, some of whom had some strong views, were able to lay those views down and say, okay, let’s pause that view, let’s tone that view down, so that we can work together to spread the news of Jesus Christ. That’s impressive. So for instance, Hans Hut had a radical view. You could imagine that to them the whole world could look like it’s coming apart. And for people like Hans Hut, this is the end times. Jesus is coming back. We tend to think of this whole end times thinking that we hear a lot right now, especially as we’re recording this. That was not uncommon back then, I suppose. So he would have been one of those guys. He would have been one of the main ones. And he actually had a date. When did he say it was going to end? He said 1528, Pentecost. Jesus is coming back. And so that gave him a passion: we’ve got to hurry and do this. So they did ask him to tone it down. They said, okay, we don’t know that. Can you tone that down? And he agreed he’d tone that down. 6:43 | The Three Baptisms And then the record of the kind of gospel they were preaching is just very challenging. Again, Hans Hut stands out as one of the more extreme. For instance, he had this message of the three baptisms. He said there is the baptism of water. There is the baptism of the Spirit, where you get this anointing. And then there is the baptism of fire, where we are willing to die. And he was telling these men, we’ve got to be willing, as we go out to the mission field, to be ready to die. In that day, if you look at the averages, of these 60 who gathered here, within the next five years it seems that only two are still alive. So that’s the kind of zeal they would have had in a little house just like this, which is really remarkable. 7:42 | The Success They Couldn’t Explain And then here’s the thing: the success. We know by the city records here in Augsburg that two weeks later there is documented proof of arrests happening as a result of the things that were decided here. They actually could not understand how it could be possible that in the time it took to come into a house and preach the gospel, and spies and others were watching, the next thing you know that person is willing to die, and joins the Anabaptists and goes with them. It reminds me of when you look at Jesus, his call to Matthew: follow me. And they just get up and go. That is documented not just from the Anabaptist writings, but from the secular writings that we have here, of how quick they were. As a matter of fact, there was a statement going around: watch out for these Anabaptists. They must have some sort of flask with a potion, and they’ll go into one of these little houses and give you the potion, and it’s going to turn you into an Anabaptist. It’s got to be that, because there’s no way they could convert someone raised in a whole other way. 8:51 | Schiemer’s Flask And one of my favorite quotes of this era is by the missionary and early Anabaptist Leonhard Schiemer. He wrote a response to this accusation, a reply to those who say we drink something from a small flask, of which the devil himself does not know what it contains. And with what you just said, the emotions of that, the likelihood that you’re not coming back, it’s pretty powerful. Let me give you this. It’s an actual Hutterite hymn, translated for us, for the sending service of missionaries. It’s rich in their theology and their feelings. I’ll read you the stanzas: 49:40 | Summing Up an Era And finally, summing up an era in the Chronicles. You get to this place where they’re summing up this whole piece, and they wanted to give a cap on what the early first generation looked like. Here’s what it says in the Chronicles: And he continues: 51:00 | What Was Lost, and What Came Back This is a unique window in time in history, when this was happening. Incredible zeal, but also incredible intentionality. There are lots of people who may say, I’m really passionate about doing ministry, but then maybe it doesn’t have the intentionality these people had. They bring them together and send them out, and 80 percent of them don’t come back. But that only happened for a time, and then it got lost. What happened? For them it went on pretty solid for about 100 years at least, until they were just literally beaten down to a pulp, and they end up, from disease and famine, as a tiny group out in what’s modern day Romania. And it finally had a new revival that brought it all back again, coming up to today, this mission zeal that was very clear and a priority. And in these quotes, how many times did the phrase “by the commandments of Christ” come out? It just comes out that you cannot be a real community unless this is part of the package. And no throwing stones. I’m looking at my life and I’m thinking, yeah, I’m going to do some evangelism. Do you put it in the calendar? Yes, I want to do something. Do you have the calling? Yes. Those things and those challenges are, yeah. I’m looking at myself. 52:17 | A Letter from Prison I guess I’ll close with this last quote. It’s from a letter that was found. This was a schoolteacher who was out as a missionary and then caught. So he’s captured, and he’s in a prison very much like this one. And he writes a letter back to the colony: It’s quite a quote. May God give us grace to do it. 54:13 | Next Episode: Melchior Hoffman and John Calvin In the next episode, we return to Strasbourg, where the Anabaptist radical Melchior Hoffman stirred the city with apocalyptic visions of Christ’s imminent return. At the same time, another voice was rising in influence: John Calvin, who was writing his first work against the Anabaptists. Two men, two very different responses to the same restless age, and both leaving deep marks on the Anabaptist movement as it pressed its way north along the Rhine River and into the Netherlands.
