title: “They Overturn All Civil Order”
description: Anabaptists & John Calvin Found Shelter at Strasbourg. The Calm Would Not Last
text: Episode 06      |    Melchior Hoffman, John Calvin “They Overturn All Civil Order” Anabaptists & John Calvin Found Shelter at Strasbourg. The Calm Would Not Last 43 min 1530–1543 Strasbourg, France About This Episode The Anabaptist story moves north in this episode, into the Low Countries, what is today the Netherlands, Belgium, and Luxembourg. But here, the story turns complicated. Not all influential Anabaptist leaders had sound theology; some drifted to extreme positions. Melchior Hoffman represents this complex nature. Dean Taylor, Stephen Russell, and Reagan Schrock dig into his complex legacy, from his legitimate contributions to the Anabaptist movement that helped launch the Dutch Anabaptist church while also staking his credibility on prophecies of Christ’s return that never came true. Hoffman returned to Strasbourg, France, and requested the authorities imprison him. Why would anyone do that? Meanwhile, also in Strasbourg, John Calvin was watching the Anabaptists. What did he make of them? What did Calvin actually write about the Schleitheim Confession? And as Calvinism spread, what did it cost the early Anabaptist movement? View Episode Credits Here: anabaptistorigins.org/credits/ Read the Transcript 0:00 | Cold Open: The Clocks of Charles V In his final days, the man who once ruled over the Holy Roman Empire sat surrounded by clocks. Some say Charles V tried obsessively to make them all chime in harmony: ticking, ringing, refusing to agree. He tried to fix them, but they just wouldn’t obey. Much like Europe. Everything was slipping. Charles could only sit and listen to the reformers he had failed to silence, to the ringing, like his clocks, just out of tune. Two of the clocks most out of sync were an Anabaptist named Melchior Hoffman and a reformer named John Calvin. 1:14 | People Who Shaped Us Without Being Our Heroes In this episode we’re going to be looking at people who maybe aren’t necessarily our heroes, but who did still shape us. That’s right. The Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 11 even says there must also be heresies among you, so that they which are approved may be manifested. And so there’s something written into the idea of the church. God seems to allow people to come and go. Even in the early church, some people came and went. Some were truly seekers who left. Some were misguided. And there were others, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, who literally sought to stop them and to destroy them. But even the worst, even those who sought to write things against the church and say things against it, that has a purifying effect. It’s like fire purifying metal: it allows the pure to come out and burns off the dross. So I think that’s what we’re seeing, and what we’re going to focus on a little bit in this episode. One of them in particular I wouldn’t put in the category of out to destroy, but maybe one who, in our opinion, would be a little misguided. We wouldn’t completely approve of him. But he’s a very fascinating person nonetheless, and that is the story of Melchior Hoffman. 2:45 | A Furrier from the Baltics Stephen, talk to us a little about Melchior Hoffman and how he ends up here in Strasbourg. Melchior Hoffman was from southern Germany. His vocation was furrier. He bought and sold furs, which put him up in the Baltic region. So he’s not a priest or anything, not someone from the church. No, he’s a layman. But he’s up in the northern part of Europe, up in the Baltics, and as he hears Luther’s teachings he likes them, and he becomes a lay preacher. But he has conflict with the Lutheran preachers already in the Baltic region. Luther tries to tone down the problem. He actually tells him to come, and then he approves of him. And so he goes back and continues to have friction with the Lutheran preachers up in the north. Part of it is that he has an apocalyptic vision of the end: it’s going to happen soon. He is apparently a good preacher, but he doesn’t agree with Luther. He’s more Zwinglian when it comes to how to look at the Lord’s Supper. And it’s things like that that cause Luther to say no. It’s amazing. He was literally thinking Christ would come in 1533. I can imagine what Luther thought. Here was going to be someone on his side, and we’re not supposed to be having different opinions. There’s an interesting quote directly from Luther about him. Writing to the authorities, Luther said, “Let not this fanatic continue to spread his illusions. He must be restrained before greater harm is done.” So in 1529 we know that Hoffman finally finds his way to Strasbourg. And even before he comes here he shifts. Because Luther has spoken so strongly against him, he shifts toward Zwinglianism, which is more or less where the reformers here in Strasbourg are. 4:42 | Strasbourg’s Moderation When he came here, again like we said in the earlier episode about Michael Sattler, Strasbourg had a moderate view comparatively, when you look at the views different places held. And Bucer and Capito tried to work with that. We’re going to see later in this episode that John Calvin himself ends up coming here for a while, and it’s interesting, his opinion of these reformers. You can see him being annoyed by some of this moderation. So that’s the world here. You see that in the letters with Sattler, with Marpeck, and now even trying to work with Hoffman. It’s sort of impressive. 5:21 | Where the Teaching Goes Strange So what you’re describing so far doesn’t sound like a terrible example for us, necessarily. Where do Hoffman’s teachings start getting a little strange? Because that comes into the picture. What were some of those teachings? Well, as I said, when he got here he was Zwinglian. Then he meets the Anabaptists, and he feels like they’re very close to him. Remember, he’s emphasizing the interior. So the Anabaptists here in the city are influencing him, and he does get baptized. Probably the biggest problem was his openness to visions and his apocalyptic view of the world, that the end is coming soon. In fact, that was something other Anabaptists said: we can’t really say that. When he meets Caspar Schwenckfeld, he accepts the concept of the celestial flesh, which is that Christ is not a human derived from one of us. He’s not derived from Mary. And that causes a real problem. Interestingly enough, we’re going to see that Hoffman goes and starts the Anabaptist movement in the north, and we’re going to find that it’s only the Dutch and North German Anabaptists who hold to this celestial flesh. The Catholics, the Protestants, and the Anabaptists from South Germany and Switzerland all say no: Jesus got his humanity from Mary, and that means he’s one of us. 6:47 | North to Emden and the Netherlands So Hoffman is getting some odd ideas about the incarnation. Where does he go then? Does he stay here, or journey on? What’s the next phase of his story? He goes north, and he does baptize. He goes to Emden, which is way in the north of Germany, just on the border with the Netherlands, and he establishes a congregation that’s still there. So that would be the first Dutch or North German Anabaptist congregation. From there he goes into the Netherlands and has a really fruitful ministry. We already talked about how the Tyrol was very fruitful in the south. Well, for some reason the Netherlands was very fruitful as a mission field in the north, and he won a lot of people to the Anabaptist position. There is a difference, though. All of the South German and Swiss Anabaptists and the Moravians were about forming a church of true believers. His baptism was about identifying people he thought would be on the Lord’s side when he returns. He wasn’t concerned about starting a church and what that would mean, that we have discipline and discipleship and so on. He thought the Lord was coming back soon, so he’s just trying to identify: these are people who are faithful. So a radically different view of church. I feel like I almost need a second to get my head around that perception of how church should be. So this is where the influence of somebody who came through and did things still left an influence, and dropped seeds that were then picked up and became very fruitful. This helps me see. We’re here in Strasbourg. How did it get from down here, the Anabaptists here, all the way north to the Netherlands? We’re saying Hoffman. That was his stomping ground, so to speak. He had been in Emden when he was still a Zwinglian, before he came to Strasbourg. 8:53 | The Stillstand This is an incredibly influential figure. He touched a lot of lives. And the people he converted and baptized, and the people those converts baptized, looked to him for leadership. When a few of his followers, the Melchiorites, were killed in Amsterdam, he called for a Stillstand, which is simply a cessation. We’re going to stop baptizing for two years, because it was unsettling to see these people executed. So after that Stillstand, some of his converts were martyred, and that shook him up, and he decided, I think we’ve reached the number of the elect, and so now we’re ready for the end. He was very apocalyptic, and there were prophecies during that time. Some of them held that he and another person might be like the two witnesses at the end of Revelation. And although he did flatly deny in some of his writings that he was Enoch or Elijah, still he published prophecies about himself and that whole thing of the coming of Christ. The clock was ticking. 10:00 | Put Me in Prison So he comes back to Strasbourg with a plan that’s a little odd. He was thinking that in this waiting period, when we’re going to see the coming of Christ and the Elijah figure coming out and showing us that Christ is coming, I need to be in prison. So he goes to the authorities and just says, put me in prison. It’s like, why do you want us to put you in prison? They didn’t for a while, and finally they agreed and said okay, we’ll put you in prison. And that’s where he sat. This is part of the old waterworks, and you can come up on top. You can literally walk on it. It’s a beautiful view. But if you had been Melchior Hoffman, this wouldn’t have been such a great view. He was probably in prison in something like one of those two towers. They date to the right time, but we don’t know if that’s where he was. He thought, because of a prophecy, that he should be in prison half a year and the Lord would come back. Well, that didn’t happen. He ended up in prison for ten years or so, and he died in prison. 11:03 | The Leadership Shifts to Jan Matthijs Hoffman had exercised a lot of authority, a lot of influence and leadership. But when he was here for more than half a year and the prophecy didn’t happen, the leadership shifted over to a man in the Netherlands, Jan Matthijs. And he believed we’ve waited long enough. The state is being violent toward us. We need to defend ourselves. Plus, Strasbourg here was supposed to be the New Jerusalem. Well, the Lord didn’t come back. Matthijs thought it would be Münster. Münster becomes the New Jerusalem, and we’ll talk more about it, but he ends up going there, and they try to make it into an Anabaptist city to which the Lord can come and establish his kingdom on the earth. So what did Hoffman think of that? He’s sitting in prison. Does he hear about this? He hears about it, and he tells them this is not the right way to go. Violence is not the right way to go. But he’s lost his influence, because what he said would happen didn’t. We do have him on record criticizing those things, saying that they’re relying on the old covenant, those kinds of things. And they were. There is something good that came out of his evangelizing up north, and that was Obbe and Dirk Philips. They never went that violent route, and there were others too who never went that violent route. So there was a kind of seedbed there for Menno to take advantage of. And we’ll talk about that when we talk about Menno. 12:37 | John Calvin Arrives In the late 1530s, just as the Anabaptists were getting past their first decade of persecution, a new threat came on the Anabaptists: John Calvin. And not just Calvin, but Calvinism. And we’re in a pretty significant spot for that. This is Strasbourg, France, and right there is the first church John Calvin preached in here in Strasbourg. He would have lived here for a while, is my understanding. Lay out some context. What did John Calvin do here? Where is he coming into this story? A generation after Luther, Protestantism took on a new form. It created a system, a system that could be imported to other countries. And one of the architects of that system was John Calvin. Born in 1509 in northern France, he started out as a person raised in the church. He studied for the priesthood, and then he studied law. But in the 1520s he started to get into the different things happening in the Reformation, and he got excited about it. In 1533 he came to the University of Basel, and it was there that he formally broke with the Catholic system and started to enter into the Protestant world. In 1536 he wrote his famous Institutes of the Christian Religion, a small book, but loaded. In that book he laid out a system of doctrine and theology, very rich in the sovereignty of God and providence and those things. But he also mixed with it a connection with the state, and it was that connection between faith and the state that made Calvinism so popular with all the different leaders around Europe. 14:09 | Geneva, and Farel’s Oath In that same year, 1536, he was traveling, and he made it to Geneva. There he met the reformer Farel, and Farel took a liking to Calvin, a big liking. As Calvin was passing through, Farel was so impressed with him that he challenged him and said, you need to stay here. As a matter of fact, he made almost a vision of it, like he’s hearing from God, a solemn oath: if you don’t come here and stay in the Reformation in Geneva, God’s going to curse you and curse your time and your leisure and your studies, and it won’t work out for you. So under that pressure, the young John Calvin accepted. As he brought in those reforms in Geneva, trying out some of these ideas of discipline and church life in the city, finally the people of Geneva had enough of John Calvin, and they ousted him. As he left, he ended up having the protection of Bucer here in Strasbourg. He came here, and this, as you brought out, is the first church he preached in, right here in Strasbourg, France. 15:08 | Writing Against the Anabaptists What year did John Calvin arrive in Strasbourg? He came here in 1538, and that’s when he preached his first sermon here. And while he was here he also did some interesting things. He expanded the Institutes of the Christian Religion. He had some time to write. And then, particularly important, he translated it into French. That made it something the common people could read and understand, and it got popular in different places. It was during that time that he also started writing about the Anabaptists. He obviously met the Anabaptists here in Strasbourg and started to pen some of his writings against them. His book, with an interesting title, written in 1549, was entitled Brief Instruction to Arm All the Good Faithful Against the Errors of the Common Sect of the Anabaptists. He wasn’t the first one to write against the Anabaptists. As we saw in Zurich, even Heinrich Bullinger in 1531 wrote one on the shameless wickedness of the Anabaptists. 16:06 | Calvin Looks for a Wife Not only was he developing his religion and his idea of the church-state and his Institutes, he was also looking for a wife. And he had some particular requirements for what he was looking for. So he wrote back to his friend and admirer Farel, back in Geneva, and in his letter this is what he said he was looking for: “The only beauty which allures me is this: that she be chaste, obliging, not too fussy, economical, patient, and careful for my health.” So guess what. Out of all the women he could look for here in Strasbourg, he ended up finding an Anabaptist woman he wanted to marry. He ended up marrying the widow of an Anabaptist preacher here in Strasbourg. 16:49 | Back to Geneva, and Servetus So then, after all that, in 1541 he gets called back to Geneva. Steve, tell us a little about his relationship there in Geneva and what he created there. The reason he was invited back was that the cardinal who had authority over Geneva wrote to the Genevans and requested that they come back to the Catholic Church. They didn’t know exactly how to answer him, so they asked Calvin to come back and take care of that. And he did. Then he established a very structured church system. He expected the church and state to work together, hand in hand. There still was some dislike toward Calvin. What settled that was an anti-Trinitarian named Servetus, who was living in France. He was from Spain, but he was living in France at the time. The Inquisition was hot on his heels, and he wanted to go to Italy, where he thought he’d be safer. For some reason he chose to come through Geneva, and he was actually listening to Calvin preach when he was recognized. He was taken prisoner. He was tried. He was found guilty of heresy. They asked both Protestant and Catholic universities what they should do with him. They ended up burning him. Calvin asked for mercy, cut his head off instead, but they went with the traditional approach, which was to burn a heretic that bad, who didn’t believe in the Trinity. The people who opposed Calvin had sort of tried to support Servetus, and that put them in a bad light. So from then on, Calvin had pretty free rein in the city as far as what he wanted to do. 18:35 | When the Councils Overlap So that goes into this system he created, and you’re bringing out very nicely the problems it created. He had this council of church members that was sort of like a Jewish Sanhedrin, if you will. And then they expected to turn that over to the city council, which would then do things like executions. The church didn’t kill people. The church handed the heretics over to the state. But the complicating thing in his system, particularly as Geneva became more and more of a Reformed state, is that church members were part of the city council. And making it even more complicated, sometimes the same person was on the church council and the city council, which confused this whole thing. That makes it difficult when you mix church and state together. That’s giving us some nice context. Calvin being here in Strasbourg, and the whole part about him marrying an Anabaptist widow, is kind of wild. I didn’t realize that until we were researching for this. It’s like, no way. What an interesting connection. 19:34 | Pushing North to the Low Countries From here, these ideas are spreading north. Do you want to say a little more about that, and how we want to dig into that as well? Let’s dig into that, because what we’ve been trying to do in this episode is take us north. We did Hoffman just now, and that takes us north. We see his influences up there, which eventually lit the fire for two strains: a radical strain, but also the conversion of Menno Simons, through his different influences up there. But also influencing the north is Calvin and Calvinism, particularly the northern part of Brussels, what’s called the Flanders area. That area was a rich place of early Anabaptism, and everything changes when Calvinism starts to go there, with all the militancy and power that comes with it. As Anabaptism pushed north along the Rhine River, the message carried by Hoffman and others found fertile ground in Flanders and the Low Countries, what is today Belgium and the southern Netherlands. The movement spread rapidly among urban craftsmen and weavers, even as troops from the Habsburg Empire moved in to crush dissent with systematic brutality. Then Calvin’s teachings arrived, and when they did, two very different worlds met: the Anabaptists, with their voluntary, disciplined communities of faith, and Calvin, with his emerging vision of a Reformed state church. Their collision marked one of the most turbulent chapters in the story of Christianity’s northern frontier. 21:38 | How Calvin Saw the Anabaptists You had a couple of quotes you wanted to read to us, because Calvin wrote about the Anabaptists and had a lot of critiques and opinions. Let’s hit some of those before we get into the story of heading north. I think it would be good for us to hear how Calvin saw the Anabaptists. Calvin and Menno were basically contemporaries. Calvin berated the Anabaptists as those who give rise to a whole sea of insane views. He felt that the Anabaptists actually favored the Catholics on certain points. I’ll give you a quote: “With regard to those poor, fantastic ones who thus pride themselves that God’s Word is on their side, facts reveal the actual case. For a long time we have labored continually to support that the Holy Word should be returned to a place of preeminence, and we have undertaken a battle against all the world to achieve this. But they, what have they done to advance this, or in what way have they helped? Rather, to the contrary, they have impeded and troubled us to such an extent that no one can say wherein they have profited, unless it lies in deferring to the Word once it has been advanced by us.” “Moreover, on several principal points of Christianity, they agree closely with the Papists,” the Catholics, “holding a view directly repugnant to all the Holy Scriptures, as with free will, predestination, and the cause of our salvation. It is therefore with deception that they abuse this pretext, making the simple believe that they wish to be governed totally according to the Scripture, for they do not hold to it whatsoever, but only to the fantasy of their own brains.” 23:19 | Calvin Reads Schleitheim Calvin, Luther, and Zwingli all felt that the Anabaptists disrupted society. Here is something Calvin said about this. And let me say, this is written about the Schleitheim Confession. So he had read the Schleitheim Confession. And he doesn’t like it. For some reason my brain just never thought of that happening. But Michael Sattler came through here in Strasbourg, which is where we are right now, and Calvin’s here in Strasbourg. So he would have read Schleitheim. He read Schleitheim. He writes: “Thus we have to consider whether Christianity and the office of justice, or temporal power, are incompatible things, so much so that if a man chooses the one, he must reject the other.” So this deals with the sword. Calvin says the Christian can pick up the sword. Schleitheim said no. It was obvious to Calvin that “these miserable fanatics have no other goal than to put everything into disorder, to undo the commonwealth of property in such a way that whoever has the power to take anything, he is welcome to it.” That is fascinating. Can you still get the book he wrote against the Anabaptists? I’m sure you can get it online somewhere. I’m kind of tempted to read it now. He has some very strong statements, like, we are the defenders of Holy Scripture, and these people are ruining this good work that we’re doing. 24:45 | Free Will, and Where the Anabaptists Sat If you remember, Bucer and Capito liked Sattler, but they felt he was wrong on certain points. Bucer didn’t specify, but I’m absolutely sure it’s the same thing Calvin cared about: free will, predestination. That was at the heart of every Protestant state church. And that’s the Catholic side he’s talking about, because the Catholics believed in free will, and the Anabaptists believed in free will. Those are the repugnant doctrines he speaks of. But he is actually right. The Anabaptists did, and do, agree with the Catholics more in some areas than in others. The Catholics have a kind of soft view of predestination, not at all like the Calvinists or the Lutherans. The Anabaptists would have said, we have free will, and the Catholics said that too. Some aspects of the devotional life that the Anabaptists maintained actually root themselves in the medieval, and therefore Catholic, devotional life. So there were several different things that made the Anabaptists in certain areas more like the Catholics. But in other areas they were clearly against the Catholics. I haven’t read everything the Anabaptists have written, but everything I’ve read that deals with their opinion of the Protestants, they almost always say, you Protestants started well, but you didn’t go far enough. And everything I’ve ever read about their response to Catholicism is, these aren’t true Christians. Just another thing: the creeds come from, whether you want to say the Catholic Church or the ancient church, and they were carried on by the Catholics. So there’s some alignment there. 26:39 | Flanders: Weavers and Tailors So we’ve got Calvinism coming onto the scene now. You’ve got the spread of Anabaptist teachings going up north into the Netherlands, and then Calvinism starts getting transported up north as well. What happens next? Where does the story go from here? We’re getting into a whole different community of Anabaptists, and it’s a whole different world. Calvinism plays a part in this, and it creates a world for the Anabaptists unexpectedly. The area we go to now is modern-day northern Belgium. It was called the Flanders area. This was an area that had a lot of Anabaptists. There were also different Reformed groups there, and some of the records make it seem sort of fluid. They were communities that were meeting and holding discussions about faith, and it was also a very prosperous area. There are a couple of quotes here that might kick us off on the discussion of the Flanders area. This one is by John D. Roth, in his book on beliefs. He talks about the Low Countries, the Netherlands. He says urban Anabaptists in the Low Countries were often more moderate in tone and more literate than the rural Swiss groups, and that the Dutch tradition produced a highly articulate theological and devotional literature already by the mid-sixteenth century. And then a quote from C. Arnold Snyder on the same area says that in Flanders, the most common occupations among the Anabaptists were weavers, tailors, and other crafts tied to the urban textile industry. If you looked at the most developed cities of their time, places like Antwerp, and even Ghent, where Charles V came from, these would have been very prosperous areas now enjoying the Dutch trade and the different things that were happening. And all that affects the early part of the Anabaptists. 28:31 | The Major Reform Movement in the North Brother Stephen, tell us a little more about all the different areas in the Netherlands and Flanders. We’ve talked about Hoffman already, and he is the one who brings a kind of Anabaptism to the north, to the Low Countries. That leads to Münster, and then we’re going to talk about how Menno and others rescued Anabaptism from that catastrophe. But it’s interesting: from the time Hoffman arrived in the Netherlands, in the Low Countries, until about the middle of the 1550s or so, Anabaptism was the major reform movement in those areas. There were some Lutherans. These are guesstimates, but 20 percent or more, in some areas more, but maybe 20 percent of the people in the Low Countries were Anabaptists at one point. And when we say Low Countries, geographically it’s kind of backwards for us, because they’re in the north. So the Netherlands, Belgium, and Luxembourg. Netherlands literally means low country. It’s off the mountains. Holland means the same thing. It means the land that’s in a hole. So the 20 percent, at least in some areas, is striking, because if you go there today it’s obviously not 20 percent. Probably in 1600, 160,000 Dutch people were baptized Anabaptists, and now it’s in the low thousands. 30:09 | The Beeldenstorm, 1566 So looking at that whole area, one event changed the attitude of it all. We had this growth all the way through the 1520s, thirties, and forties, and now we get to the 1560s, and things start to go pretty awry in the Flanders area and in other parts of the Netherlands. Calvinism’s now growing. Around Flanders you have whole big assemblies of people, street preaching, people watching, and they’re getting excited, talking about this new way. And it gets bad. Then a particular event happens in 1566 that history has called the Beeldenstorm. It’s the iconoclast takeover of the churches in Flanders and the different parts of the Netherlands. And this was bad. It was real bad. In 1566, mobs of people swept through hundreds of churches in Flanders and the Dutch provinces, destroying images, tearing things down. It was terrible. Interestingly enough, there is not a documented record of any Anabaptists either discussing it, planning it, or even being captured during those raids. It’s fair to say that people who were sliding between the different forms were part of it, but for the record, there were none there. But this caused a reaction from the imperial court, and they struck back hard. The records of this are really sad. Here’s an actual account written by a peasant in Antwerp. As he was looking at what was happening, he said it looked like hell. He looked at the churches filled with ten thousand torches, the sounds of falling statues and shattered organ pipes. He even said that walking through the wreckage was nearly impossible just due to the scale of the destruction. It sounds like literally a bomb had gone off in some of these places. 32:07 | The Council of Blood So in response, King Philip II of Spain sent the Duke of Alva with 10,000 troops marching on Flanders, saying, okay, enough of this Protestantism, we’re going to wipe it out.
